senses.definition: Six tricks taken by one side.
senses.example: By taking six tricks in the last hand, Dad made book and won the rubber.

senses.definition: Four of a kind.
senses.example: My opponent showed a book of kings, beating my full house.

senses.definition: The list of mares that a stallion will breed in a given season.
senses.example: The stallion's book was full, so the breeder turned away three mares this season.

senses.definition: A list of the races that a jockey is scheduled to ride in.
senses.example: Her book for Saturday includes six races at Belmont, starting before noon.

senses.definition: The twenty-sixth Lenormand card.
senses.example: The reader laid the Book card beside the Lady, then turned over the Clover.

senses.definition: Any source of instruction.
senses.example: The manual was my only book on wiring, so I learned everything from it.

senses.definition: The accumulated body of knowledge passed down among black pimps.
senses.example: Nobody learns the book from a manual, he told me; you learn it on the street.

senses.definition: A portfolio of one's previous work in the industry.
senses.example: Bring your book to the interview; the designers want to see your past projects.

senses.definition: A document, held by the referee, of the incidents that happened in a game.
senses.example: The referee wrote the foul in his book and showed the captain a warning.

senses.definition: A list of all players who have been booked (received a warning) in a game.
senses.example: The coach checked the book after the match to see which players were booked.

senses.definition: The sum of chess knowledge in the opening or endgame.
senses.example: The opposite-colored bishops endgame is usually a book draw.

senses.definition: (historical) A package of silk.
senses.example: The merchant's ledger listed a book of silk shipped from Canton in 1790.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To reserve (something) for future use.
senses.example: I want to book a hotel room for tomorrow night.

senses.definition: To write down, to register or record in a book or as in a book.
senses.example: They booked that message from the hill.

senses.definition: To add a name to the list of people who are participating in something.
senses.example: I booked a flight to New York.

senses.definition: To travel very fast.
senses.example: He was really booking until he passed the speed trap.

senses.definition: To record bets as bookmaker.
senses.example: The bar owner booked bets on the Derby for anyone willing to risk twenty dollars.

senses.definition: To move or leave, often hurriedly and abruptly.
senses.example: He was here earlier, but he booked.

senses.definition: To record the name and other details of a suspected offender and the offense for later judicial action.
senses.example: The police booked him for driving too fast.

senses.definition: To issue a caution to, usually a yellow card, or a red card if a yellow card has already been issued.
To receive the highest grade in a class.
senses.example: The top three students had a bet on which one was going to book their intellectual property class.

core.definition: A collection of printed or written pages bound together along one edge, or a long written work such as a novel or textbook.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short oo of 'foot', not the long oo of 'boot'. Keep the final k crisp, with no extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word itself carries no positive or negative feeling; tone comes from the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'book' for printed volumes and for e-books alike, and it is everyday vocabulary in schools, libraries and conversation. People say 'check out a book' at a library and 'book a flight' for reserving travel. For a specific kind of book, Americans usually name it, such as 'novel', 'textbook' or 'cookbook', rather than saying 'book' alone.

distinctions.note: A novel is one specific kind of book: a long work of fiction. 'Book' is the broader word for any bound work.
A textbook is written for teaching a subject, usually in school or college, while 'book' can mean any bound work.
An e-book is the same content in digital form; Americans still often just say 'book' for both, adding 'e-' only when the format matters.

examples.everyday: I'm halfway through a great book about the Lewis and Clark trip, and I can't put it down.
examples.professional: Our editor wants the book manuscript by March, so we need the final chapters reviewed this month.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the book of Daniel was composed in the sixth or the second century BC, and the answer shapes how its visions are read.

nuance.analogy: A book is a box of ideas that opens when you turn its pages.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bōc, 'book, written document'; probably related to 'beech', since early writing was carved on beech-wood tablets.
common_mistakes: Saying 'three book' instead of 'three books' after a number
Pronouncing the vowel like the long oo in 'boot' (/buk/) instead of the short /ʊ/ in 'foot'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture a book is often a scroll or a written record of God's acts and judgments. The Hebrew word sefer and the Greek word biblion both mean a written scroll or book. The 'book of life' is a central image: Revelation 3:5 speaks of the names of the faithful not being blotted out of it, Revelation 20:12 describes the dead judged by what is written in the books and in the book of life, and Revelation 21:27 says that only those written in the Lamb's book of life may enter the holy city.

book.etymology: From Middle English *bok*, *book*, from Old English *bōc*, from **bōk*, from Proto-Germanic **bōks*.

senses.definition: A peasant.
senses.example: In the old village, a boor worked the fields from dawn until dusk.

senses.definition: A Boer, white South African of Dutch or Huguenot descent.
senses.example: Historians note that the early settlers, called boors, farmed the Cape frontier for generations.

senses.definition: A yokel, country bumpkin.
senses.example: The city visitors laughed at the boor who wore his hat indoors.

senses.definition: An uncultured person; a vulgarian.
senses.example: At the gallery opening, the boor loudly criticized the paintings and bumped into guests.

core.definition: A rude, insensitive person who lacks good manners and social polish. The word is a strong criticism.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short oo of 'book,' and the r is pronounced clearly in American English. Do not confuse it with bore, which is /bɔɹ/, or boar, which is also /bɔɹ/.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a boor is a sharp insult, usually in writing or formal criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Boor is mainly a literary or formal word. In casual American speech, people say jerk, rude guy or creep. You are more likely to meet boor in essays, reviews or classic novels than in daily conversation.

distinctions.note: Jerk is casual, everyday American slang for a rude or mean person; boor is more formal and focuses on bad manners.
A lout is a rough, crude man who behaves badly in public, often loudly or aggressively; a boor is more about rudeness and lack of refinement.
A philistine scorns art, learning or culture; a boor may be rude without caring about culture at all.

examples.everyday: The guy at the party was a total boor; he kept interrupting everyone and mocking their jokes.
examples.professional: Whatever his talent, he was a boor in meetings, cutting off junior engineers mid-sentence.
examples.analytical: Castiglione's ideal courtier stands as the opposite of the boor, the man who lacks grace and refinement.

nuance.analogy: A boor is like a loud speaker in a library, unable to notice the quiet others need.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Dutch boer, meaning farmer or peasant, which later took on the sense of a crude or uncultured person.
common_mistakes: Confusing boor with bore, the word for a dull person or a tool for drilling; they are different words.
Using boor casually in speech; in everyday American English, people usually say jerk or rude guy.

senses.definition: (obsolete) Someone given to empty boasting; a braggart.
senses.example: Ah, that braggadocian knight never stops talking about his own victories.
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: A person who boasts loudly and emptily about their abilities or achievements; a braggart.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, DOH, and the final syllable is reduced to 'un'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the ending as a full 'ee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone who is annoying because they boast without substance.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare variant of 'braggadocio' and is not common in American speech. Americans would normally say 'braggart' or 'show-off'. You may see it in literature or older dictionaries, but in conversation use 'braggart' instead.

distinctions.note: Braggart is the common everyday word for a boaster; braggadocian is rare and more literary.
Braggadocio can mean either the person or the empty boasting itself; braggadocian refers only to the person.

examples.professional: In the staff meeting, one braggadocian kept claiming credit for every project, so we need to check the actual results.
examples.analytical: The narrator's account of his exploits reveals him as a braggadocian whose claims collapse under scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like a rooster crowing loudly before the sun rises, making a lot of noise without doing the real work.
nuance.etymology: From 'braggadocio', itself coined by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene, with the suffix -ian meaning 'one who'.
common_mistakes: Using 'braggadocian' in everyday conversation where 'braggart' is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable (BRAG-uh-doh-shun) instead of DOH.

senses.definition: To feed (a baby) milk via the breasts; to suckle; to nurse.
senses.example: This is a designated place for mothers to breastfeed their babies.

senses.definition: To nurse, to suck milk from a breast.
An instance of feeding milk to a baby from the breasts; a breastfeeding.
senses.example: The nurse said the first breastfeed after delivery went much better than expected.

core.definition: To feed a baby milk directly from the mother's breast.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, BREST, with a lighter stress on FEED. In the word the s and t are clearly pronounced, so avoid dropping the t as sometimes happens in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and supportive. American health guidance encourages it, and the word is used without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use breastfeed in medical, parenting and everyday conversation, and it is the term used by pediatricians and public health groups. Nurse is also used in the same way, though many people now find it a little old-fashioned. When talking to someone, the casual question is 'Are you breastfeeding?' and a natural reply is 'Yes, it's going well' or 'We're doing it for now.'

distinctions.note: Nurse is an older and more general word that can mean feeding a baby at the breast or with a bottle in some contexts, so breastfeed is clearer in medical settings.
Formula feeding means giving a baby prepared powdered or liquid milk, while breastfeeding means giving breast milk directly.

examples.everyday: My sister is breastfeeding her newborn, so we're bringing dinner over this weekend.
examples.professional: The hospital's new policy encourages nurses to help new mothers breastfeed within the first hour after birth.
examples.analytical: The debate over whether to breastfeed in public shows how a biological act can also become a question of social norms and rights.

nuance.analogy: Breastfeeding is like a personal delivery service that is built into the body: the milk is always ready, at the right temperature, and delivered straight to the baby.
nuance.etymology: Compound of breast and feed, dating to the 19th century in English.
common_mistakes: Using breast-feed with a hyphen in modern American writing, where breastfeed is the standard spelling.
Saying 'breastfeeding a bottle' or using breastfeed for bottle feeding milk, which is incorrect.

senses.definition: In a bright manner.
senses.example: The sun was shining brightly, making me squint.

core.definition: In a way that shines with strong light, or with a cheerful, lively manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The t before the l is a clean stop, not a flap, so avoid adding an extra syllable such as 'bright-uh-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes light, color, or a cheerful expression, so the feeling depends on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brightly mostly with verbs and participles of light, color, or expression, such as 'brightly lit', 'brightly colored', or 'smiled brightly'. It works in both casual and formal speech. For a smart person, Americans use the adjective 'bright' ('She's a bright kid'), not 'brightly'.

distinctions.note: Brilliantly means with exceptional skill or dazzling effect; brightly refers only to visible light, color, or a cheerful manner.
Vividly describes strong, clear images in memory or description, while brightly is simpler and refers to light or cheerfulness.

examples.everyday: The sun was shining so brightly that we all grabbed our sunglasses.
examples.professional: The new dashboard shows the critical alerts in brightly colored bars so the on-call team spots them quickly.
examples.analytical: Plato's allegory of the cave turns on the prisoner's pain when sunlight shines brightly into eyes long used to dim shadows.

nuance.analogy: Like a lamp turned all the way up, the light hits your eyes directly and clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English beorht, bright, with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Saying 'brightly' for a smart person; Americans say 'bright' for intelligence.
Stressing the second syllable or inserting an extra vowel: 'bright-uh-lee'.

brightly.etymology: From Middle English *brightly*, from Old English *beorhtlice*, equivalent to *bright* + *-ly*.

senses.definition: The edge, margin, or border of a steep place, as of a precipice; a bank or edge.
senses.example: the brink of a river

senses.definition: The edge or border.
senses.example: the brink of success

core.definition: The edge of something dangerous, or the point just before a major change or disaster.

pronunciation.tip: It is one stressed syllable with a short i and a clear ng followed by k. Do not add an extra vowel between ng and k.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, because it usually signals danger, crisis or risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brink in news, politics and everyday talk about crises, as in on the brink of war or on the brink of collapse. It can also describe a positive turning point, but the danger sense is most common. The phrase is standard and sounds natural in both casual and serious speech.

distinctions.note: Edge is the general word for a boundary; brink suggests a dangerous or critical point, often at a steep drop.
Verge means being about to experience something, often neutral; brink often suggests danger or a dramatic turn.

examples.everyday: After the flu, I was on the brink of canceling the trip, but I felt better and went anyway.
examples.professional: The project is on the brink of missing its deadline, so we need to reassign two engineers this week.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on the claim that the nation stood on the brink of collapse, which requires careful historical evidence.

nuance.analogy: The brink is like the top of a cliff: one more step and you fall, so everything depends on where you stand.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Low German or Dutch brink, meaning a grassy edge or slope.
common_mistakes: Using on the brink without of: it must be on the brink of something.
Confusing brink with brim, the top rim of a container.

brink.etymology: From Middle English *brinke*, *brenke*, from Old Norse **brenka*, *brekka*, from Proto-Germanic **brinkǭ*, **brinkaz* (“hill, edge”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰren-* (“to project”).

senses.definition: Brute fact.
senses.example: Philosophers debate whether the boiling point of water is a brute-fact of nature.

core.definition: In philosophy, a fact that has no further explanation; it simply is the case and cannot be reduced to something more basic.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are one syllable, and the main stress usually falls on 'fact' at the end of the phrase, with 'brute' lighter. Keep the American r in 'brute' and make 'fact' short and clipped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in philosophy and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This term is used in analytic philosophy, metaphysics, and philosophy of science to describe facts that cannot be explained by other facts. Americans use it in seminars, papers, and debates, not in everyday speech. It is normally contrasted with institutional facts, which depend on human conventions.

distinctions.note: An institutional fact depends on human rules or agreements, such as a currency being money; a brute fact holds regardless of human conventions, such as the mass of a stone.
A fact is any true statement about the world; a brute fact is a special kind of fact that is ultimate and unexplained.

collocations: a brute fact about the universe
accept something as a brute fact

examples.analytical: Searle argues that the existence of physical objects is a brute fact, not something we create through social rules.

nuance.analogy: A brute fact is like a boulder sitting in a field: it is there, and asking why it is there does not lead to a further explanation.
nuance.etymology: Combines brute, from Latin brutus meaning heavy or senseless, with fact, from Latin factum meaning something done.
common_mistakes: Hyphenating inconsistently; the compound is usually written 'brute fact' as a noun phrase, with a hyphen only when used as a compound modifier.
Using it for any unexplained event in everyday speech, where the term has a precise philosophical meaning.

senses.definition: Initialism of by the way.
senses.example: BTW, the quarterly report is due Friday, so please send me your numbers today.

core.definition: Abbreviation for 'by the way', used in texts and emails to add a side comment or extra piece of information.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters B, T and W, with the main stress on DUB. Americans spell it aloud as 'bee tee double-you' in speech, but in conversation they usually say the full phrase 'by the way'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual, a signal that a side comment is coming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use BTW in texts, chat, and casual email with friends and coworkers you know well. Don't use it in formal letters, job applications, or messages to someone senior. In speech, people say 'by the way' or 'oh, also' and don't spell out the letters. A natural reply to a BTW comment is simply 'Thanks' or 'Got it'.

distinctions.note: FYI means 'for your information' and presents something relevant to act on; BTW introduces a side comment or a tangent.
P.S. comes after the closing of a letter or email; BTW appears in the middle of a message.

examples.everyday: BTW, the pizza place on Main closes at ten tonight.
examples.professional: Thanks for the pipeline update. BTW, can we move Thursday's review to two o'clock?
examples.analytical: Your proof holds for all n greater than two. BTW, the lemma you cite is from the 1962 paper, not the 1958 one.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note on the side of a document, added after the main message.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'by the way', formed from the initial letters of the phrase.
common_mistakes: Using BTW in formal writing, such as a cover letter or a message to a senior executive.
Saying the letters aloud in conversation, when Americans usually say 'by the way'.

senses.definition: Affected by a bug (computer error).
senses.example: The latest version of the software is extremely bugged.

senses.definition: Containing a bug (interceptive listening device).
senses.example: I won't speak candidly since I don't know if her apartment is bugged or not.

core.definition: Affected by a software bug, meaning a program or system contains an error that causes it to malfunction.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, rhyming with hugged. Do not add a vowel before the d, and make the final g and d sound clearly together.

nuance.connotation: Negative in the software sense, since it describes a defect. In casual speech it can also mean annoyed.
nuance.usage_note: In tech, Americans say the app or feature is bugged to mean it has defects, though buggy is more common. Outside tech, bugged means annoyed or bothered, as in 'It bugs me that the store is always closed.' Americans also use bugged to mean that a room or phone has a hidden listening device.

distinctions.note: Buggy describes code or software that contains defects in general, while bugged more often refers to a specific feature or system affected by a bug.
Glitchy means occasionally malfunctioning in a minor way, while bugged suggests a defect in the underlying software or setup.
Broken means not working at all, whereas bugged means working incorrectly because of an error.

examples.everyday: Sorry, my phone keeps freezing because the new update seems bugged.
examples.professional: The release candidate is bugged, so QA has to hold off on regression testing until the fix ships.
examples.analytical: A bugged specification may be technically correct yet still produce outcomes no one intended.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe with one wrong ingredient: the cook follows every step, but the result is off.
nuance.etymology: From bug, Middle English bugge, 'a frightening thing'; the computer-error sense spread in the mid-20th century.
common_mistakes: Using bugged to mean annoyed in formal writing; in that sense it is informal, so use bothered or annoyed instead.
Saying bug-ged with an extra syllable; it is one syllable.

senses.definition: To meet by chance.
senses.example: We bumped into each other at the library yesterday.

senses.definition: To collide with.
senses.example: He bumped into the wall. I guess that's a risk you take when you read while walking.

senses.definition: To cause (a thing) to collide with.
senses.example: The roads were so slippery that I couldn't stop, and I bumped my car into the car in front of me.

core.definition: To meet someone by chance, or to hit or collide with something by accident.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'in' more than 'bump'. In fast speech 'into' reduces to 'IN-tuh', and the p of bump links smoothly into the vowel, so it sounds like 'bump-IN-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when meaning meet by chance, and negative when meaning collide.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bump into' for running into an acquaintance, as in 'I bumped into Sarah at the gym', which is friendly and casual. The physical sense is common too, as in 'I bumped into the door'. A natural reply to news of a chance meeting is 'No way, how was she?'

distinctions.note: Run into and bump into both mean meet by chance, but bump into more often suggests a casual, unplanned encounter and is also used for physical collisions.
Meet implies being introduced or arranging a meeting, while bump into means an accidental encounter.

collocations: bump into someone at the store

examples.everyday: I bumped into Mike at Target yesterday, and we ended up talking for an hour.
examples.professional: I bumped into the data lead in the hallway, and we agreed to sync on the model drift issue tomorrow.
examples.analytical: To bump into an idea by chance is not the same as reasoning toward it, though the two can look alike in retrospect.

nuance.analogy: Think of bumping into someone like two shopping carts drifting into each other in a crowded store: it is unplanned and brief.
nuance.etymology: Bump is imitative of a dull, heavy sound, and into indicates movement toward an object.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bump to someone' instead of 'bump into someone'.
Using bump into for planned meetings, which should be 'meet up with'.
Stressing bump and reducing into so much that it sounds like 'bumpin'.

conversation.text: I bumped into my old roommate at Target yesterday.
You'll never guess who I bumped into at the airport.
Sorry, I didn't mean to bump into you.
I bumped into Ana at the mall yesterday.
It's funny how we keep bumping into each other here.

senses.definition: Someone or something that bumps.
senses.example: The stiff-armed rookie was a relentless bumper who knocked every opponent off the path.

senses.definition: A drinking vessel filled to the brim.
senses.example: At the wedding toast, the best man raised a bumper of wine.

senses.definition: Anything large or successful.
senses.example: Her first novel was a bumper, selling millions of copies within a year.

senses.definition: Parts at the front and back of a vehicle which are meant to absorb the impact of a collision; fender.
Any mechanical device used to absorb an impact, soften a collision, or protect against impact.
senses.example: The company sells screw-on rubber bumpers and feet.

senses.definition: A side wall of a pool table.
senses.example: The cue ball rebounded off the bumper along the table's edge.

senses.definition: A cylindrical object used (as a substitute for birds) to train dogs to retrieve.
senses.example: He trained the spaniel to retrieve a bumper thrown across the field.

senses.definition: A short ditty or jingle used to separate a show from the advertisements.
senses.example: The radio station played a bumper before the commercial break.

senses.definition: A covered house at a theater, etc. in honor of some favorite performer.
senses.example: Fans erected a bumper over the stage door to honor their favorite diva.

senses.definition: An object on a playfield that applies force to the pinball when hit, often giving a minor increase in score.
senses.example: The pinball flipped off a bumper, scoring fifty points instantly.

senses.definition: In National Hunt racing, a flat race for horses that have not yet competed either in flat racing or over obstacles.
senses.example: The young gelding ran in the bumper at the spring meet.

senses.definition: A shoulder button on a gamepad.
senses.example: He pressed the left bumper to aim his grenade in the shooter game.

senses.definition: Synonym of gutter guard (“rail to prevent a ball from rolling into the gutter”).
senses.example: We installed a bumper along the lane so kids could bowl without gutter balls.

senses.definition: A bouncer.
senses.example: The club hired a bumper to stand at the door and keep order.

senses.definition: An extra musician (not notated in the score) who assists the principal French horn by playing less-exposed passages, so that the principal can save their 'lip' for difficult solos. Also applied to other sections of the orchestra.
senses.example: The orchestra hired an extra bumper to cover the principal horn's hardest passages.

senses.definition: Wonderfully large; (as if) filled to the bumpers at the top of a silo, or successful in this regard.
senses.example: a bumper collection of silly jokes

core.definition: The strip of metal or plastic on the front or back of a car that absorbs the impact in a low-speed collision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an r-colored, unstressed vowel, so do not add an extra vowel before the r; the p is a light closure, not a hard 'puh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, practical. It describes a car part or a general object without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bumper for the car part everyone talks about after a fender-bender, as in 'I scraped the bumper in the parking lot.' Bumper is also used for bumper cars at amusement parks, and bumper sticker for the decal on the back of a car. The older senses, a drinking glass filled to the brim and a large or abundant thing, are rare in everyday American speech except in the phrase 'bumper crop.'

distinctions.note: In American English, a fender is the body panel over a wheel, while the bumper is the crash bar at the front or back of the car.
A bump is the event of hitting something, while a bumper is the car part designed to absorb that hit.

examples.everyday: I dented my bumper backing out of the grocery store lot.
examples.professional: This year's bumper crop of applicants forced us to tighten the screening process.
examples.analytical: A bumper is designed to crumple on impact, which spreads the force over time and reduces the damage to the frame.

nuance.analogy: Like the rubber cushions on a pool table, built to take the hit so the important parts do not get damaged.
nuance.etymology: From bump (verb) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bumber' with a b-sound at the end, instead of the p.
Using bumper for the car body panel over the wheel; Americans call that a fender.
Using bumper as a noun for a large object outside 'bumper crop' or 'bumper sticker' without a clear context.

senses.definition: Incompetently performed; ruined through incompetent action; botched up.
senses.example: The bungled repair left the kitchen sink leaking worse than before we called him.

core.definition: Done badly or incompetently, so that the result fails or is ruined.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the 'g' as a hard sound. The ending 'led' becomes a short, reduced 'uld.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes sloppy or careless work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bungled' in everyday talk, news, and workplace conversation to describe failed plans, repairs, or presentations. It is informal and can sound harsh if aimed at a specific person. A softer option is 'mishandled.'

distinctions.note: Botched is cruder and more informal, suggesting a job ruined by poor work, while bungled focuses on clumsy mistakes.
Mishandled is more neutral and often used in professional or news settings to describe poor management of a situation.

examples.everyday: The plumber bungled the installation, so now the sink leaks every time I run the water.
examples.professional: The bungled rollout forced us to roll back the update and apologize to customers.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the bungled negotiations revealed a deeper failure of planning rather than bad luck.

nuance.analogy: Like a knot tied in the wrong order that will not hold.
nuance.etymology: From the verb bungle, of uncertain origin, possibly related to Middle English bungle.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'bun-gulled' with the 'g' silent.
Using 'bungled' as a present tense verb form instead of past or adjective.

senses.definition: A continuous humming noise, as of bees; a confused murmur, as of general conversation in low tones.
senses.example: The buzz of bees filled the garden as the afternoon sun warmed the roses.

senses.definition: A whisper.
senses.example: I caught a buzz that the manager was leaving, but nobody would confirm it.

senses.definition: The audible friction of voiced consonants.
senses.example: In phonetics class, we measured the buzz of the English letter z against its voiceless partner s.

senses.definition: A rush or feeling of energy or excitement; a feeling of slight intoxication.
senses.example: Still feeling the buzz from the coffee, he pushed through the last of the homework.

senses.definition: A telephone call or e-mail.
senses.example: Give me a buzz when you land, and I'll pick you up at the curb.

senses.definition: Major topic of conversation; widespread rumor; information spread behind the scenes.
senses.example: There's a buzz around the office that the merger will finally be announced Friday.

senses.definition: Synonym of fizz-buzz (“counting game”).
senses.example: The kids played buzz on the car ride, counting up through the numbers.

senses.definition: To make a low, continuous, humming or sibilant sound, like that made by bees with their wings.
senses.example: A fly was buzzing past me.

senses.definition: To utter a murmuring sound; to speak with a low, humming voice.
senses.example: The congregation buzzed softly during the pause before the benediction.

senses.definition: Of a group of people, to talk about some interesting topic excitedly.
senses.example: After the lecture, the students buzzed about the new algorithm all through lunch.

senses.definition: To fly while making such a sound.
senses.example: A fly was buzzing past me.

senses.definition: To show a high level of activity and haste, energization or excitement, to be busy as a bee in one’s actions but perhaps mentally charged.
senses.example: The room was buzzing with excitement.

senses.definition: To whisper; to communicate, as tales, in an undertone; to spread, as a report, by whispers or secretly.
senses.example: Word buzzed through the department that layoffs were coming, though no one had confirmed it.

senses.definition: To talk to incessantly or confidentially in a low humming voice.
senses.example: My sister buzzed in my ear about her landlord all through the drive home.

senses.definition: To fly at high speed and at a very low altitude over (an area), as to make a surprise pass.
senses.example: buzzing around in small cars that dodged through traffic

senses.definition: To cut (the hair) in a close-cropped military style, or buzzcut.
senses.example: Dad buzzed his hair short before the summer, so he would not bother with combs.

senses.definition: To throw swiftly.
senses.example: The pitcher buzzed a fastball past the batter, who never saw it coming.

senses.definition: To communicate with (a person) by means of a buzzer.
senses.example: The receptionist buzzed me in through the locked door at the front of the building.

core.definition: A low, humming sound, or lively excitement and chatter about something new, popular, or interesting.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the short u of cup. The final z is voiced, like a bee's sound, not an s, so do not say it as bus.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing excitement about a product or event; neutral when describing a humming sound.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use buzz for the hum of a machine or bees, and for the excited talk about something trendy, such as 'There's a lot of buzz about the new restaurant.' It is informal and natural in both casual conversation and marketing. In business, generating buzz means creating public interest. It is not usually used for serious discussion, so saying 'the buzz on this report' would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Hum is a steady, low sound without implying excitement, while buzz can also mean social excitement.
Hype is excessive promotion, often seen as exaggerated, while buzz is a more general interest or excitement.
A drone is a monotonous, continuous sound, often negative in tone, while buzz can be lively or pleasant.

examples.everyday: There's a real buzz about the new taco place downtown, so let's try it tonight.
examples.professional: The product launch created a lot of buzz on social media before the official release.
examples.analytical: The buzz surrounding a new technology often outpaces the evidence of its actual value.

nuance.analogy: Like a beehive where everyone talks at once, a buzz is the sound of many people's energy gathering in one place.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of the sound; the word echoes the humming noise made by bees.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing buzz as bus, which changes the meaning and sounds like a vehicle.
Using buzz as a countable noun without an article in phrases like 'there is buzz' instead of 'there is a buzz.'

buzz.etymology: From Middle English **bussen* (suggested by *bussyng* (“buzzing”)), of onomatopoeic origin.

senses.definition: To thoroughly examine or investigate (something) physically or by discussion; to debate, to gather opinion, to scrutinize.
senses.example: The auditors will canvass every invoice in the ledger before releasing the quarterly report.

senses.definition: To seek or solicit donations, information, opinions, support, etc. from (people or a place)
senses.example: The police are canvassing the neighborhood for information about the missing child.

senses.definition: To seek the support of (voters or a constituency) in a forthcoming election or poll through personal solicitation or public addresses.
senses.example: The electoral candidate canvassed the district for votes.

senses.definition: To toss (someone) in a (canvas) sheet for fun or as a punishment; to blanket.
senses.example: The rowdy campers canvassed the new counselor in a blanket as a welcome prank.

senses.definition: To batter, beat, or thrash (someone or something).
senses.example: The bully canvassed the younger boy behind the gym, leaving him bruised and crying.

senses.definition: To assail or attack (someone or something).
senses.example: Rebel forces canvassed the outpost at dawn, overwhelming the small garrison.

senses.definition: To severely criticize (a person, a written work, etc.).
senses.example: The reviewer canvassed the novel so harshly that the author withdrew it from shelves.

senses.definition: To debate, to discuss.
senses.example: The two committee members canvassed the budget proposal late into the evening.

senses.definition: To seek or solicit donations, information, opinions, support, etc. to conduct a survey.
senses.example: Volunteers canvassed the neighborhood door to door to gather signatures for the survey.

senses.definition: To seek the support of voters or a constituency in a forthcoming election or poll; to campaign.
senses.example: She canvassed hard across three counties, hoping to win the party's Senate nomination.

senses.definition: A seeking or solicitation of donations, information, opinions, support, etc.
senses.example: The church's annual canvass raised enough money to repair the bell tower roof.

senses.definition: A seeking or solicitation, or determination, of support or favorable votes in a forthcoming election or poll.
senses.example: Her canvass of the district showed strong support among young voters.

senses.definition: A scrutiny of the votes cast in an election to reject irregular votes; also, a tally, audit, and certification of votes.
senses.example: The county board ordered a canvass of the ballots after the close race.

senses.definition: A thorough discussion or investigation. (Possibly; the meaning is unclear.)
senses.example: The committee's canvass of the evidence lasted three days and resolved little.

senses.definition: Rejection (at an election, of a suit, etc.).
senses.example: The clerk's canvass of the petition resulted in its rejection without a hearing.

core.definition: To go through an area or group of people asking for votes, donations, or opinions, often door to door.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the second vowel to a schwa so the word sounds like 'KAN-vus.' It sounds exactly like canvas, the cloth, so pay attention to the context.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a common civic or business activity, though it can feel pushy when someone calls at home.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use canvass most often in politics, such as 'the campaign is canvassing the neighborhood' or 'volunteers went out to canvass.' It also appears in business and fundraising, as in 'canvassing for donations.' A common reply to a canvasser at the door is 'No thanks, I'm not interested,' or 'I already voted.'

distinctions.note: To poll means to collect opinions through a survey or question list, while to canvass means going out to people in person or by phone to ask.
To solicit means to ask for something in general, such as donations, business, or help, and it has no specific connection to voting.
Canvas is the cloth or painting surface, and it is a homophone of canvass, so the meaning depends entirely on context.

examples.everyday: A volunteer came by to canvass for the school board candidate, and I actually talked to her for a while.
examples.professional: The fundraising team will canvass the top twenty donors this month, so please update the contact list by Friday.
examples.analytical: To canvass a population is to sample opinion through direct contact, which makes the method intimate but also prone to selection bias.

nuance.analogy: To canvass is like walking every hallway of a building with a clipboard, knocking on each door to ask a question.
nuance.etymology: From an older sense meaning to toss in a canvas sheet or to examine closely, from canvas, the cloth.
common_mistakes: Confusing canvass with canvas, which is a different noun, even though they sound the same.
Using canvass for a formal poll or survey conducted by mail, which is better described as a poll or survey.

canvass.etymology: The verb is derived from *canvas* (“type of coarse cloth woven from hemp”).

senses.definition: A close-fitting hat, either brimless or peaked.
senses.example: The children were all wearing caps to protect them from the sun.

senses.definition: A special hat to indicate rank, occupation, etc.
senses.example: The fire chief wore a white cap that signaled his rank at the parade.

senses.definition: An academic mortarboard.
senses.example: The graduates tossed their caps into the air at the end of the ceremony.

senses.definition: A protective cover or seal.
senses.example: He took the cap off the bottle and splashed himself with some cologne.

senses.definition: A crown for covering a tooth.
senses.example: He had golden caps on his teeth.

senses.definition: The summit of a mountain, etc.
senses.example: There was snow on the cap of the mountain.

senses.definition: An artificial upper limit or ceiling.
senses.example: We should put a cap on the salaries, to keep them under control.

senses.definition: The top part of a mushroom.
senses.example: The mushroom's cap was smooth and brown, so I picked it for the soup.

senses.definition: A small amount of percussive explosive in a paper strip or plastic cup for use in a toy gun.
senses.example: Billy spent all morning firing caps with his friends, re-enacting storming the beach at Normandy.

senses.definition: A small explosive device used to detonate a larger charge of explosives.
senses.example: He wired the cap to the bundle of dynamite, then detonated it remotely.

senses.definition: A bullet used to shoot someone.
senses.example: The officer heard a cap crack through the window and dove for cover.

senses.definition: A lie or exaggeration.
senses.example: no cap

senses.definition: A place on a national team; an international appearance.
senses.example: Rio Ferdinand won his 50th cap for England in a game against Sweden.

senses.definition: Something covering the top or end of a thing for protection or ornament.
senses.example: Put a cap on the bottle to keep the sauce from spilling in your bag.

senses.definition: A portion of a spherical or other convex surface.
senses.example: The volume of the spherical cap can be computed from its height and base radius.

senses.definition: A large size of writing paper.
senses.example: flat cap; foolscap; legal cap

senses.definition: Popcorn.
senses.example: At the fair, Dad bought a bag of cap and we ate it all during the parade.

senses.definition: Capitalization.
senses.example: Check the cap on the names before you send the report.

senses.definition: A capital letter.
senses.example: Start every sentence with a cap, and end it with a period.

senses.definition: A capacitor.
senses.example: parasitic caps

senses.definition: Clipping of capture; a recording or screenshot.
senses.example: Anyone have a cap of the games last night?

senses.definition: A capsule of a drug.
senses.example: The pharmacist handed me a cap of antibiotic and told me to take it with food.

senses.definition: A capitalist.
senses.example: The old cap in the financial district still wanted to fund the startup.

senses.definition: A caption.
senses.example: Read the cap under the photo to learn where the picture was taken.

senses.definition: A cappuccino.
senses.example: I'll take a cap with oat milk, extra foam, and no sugar, please.

senses.definition: The whole top of the head of a bird from the base of the bill to the nape of the neck.
senses.example: The cardinal's bright red cap made him easy to spot in the snowy hedge.

senses.definition: The uppermost of any assemblage of parts.
senses.example: the cap of a column, door, etc.; a capital, coping, cornice, lintel, or plate

senses.definition: A collar of iron or wood used in joining spars, as the mast and the topmast, the bowsprit and the jib boom; also, a covering of tarred canvas at the end of a rope.
senses.example: The sailor fitted a new iron cap to join the topmast to the mast.

senses.definition: A capillary.
senses.example: Doctors measured blood flow through the tiny cap near the skin surface.

senses.definition: To cover or seal with a cap.
To award a cap as a mark of distinction.
To lie over or on top of something.
To paint over someone else's piece or tag.
To surpass or outdo.
To set (or reach) an upper limit on something.
senses.example: to cap wages

senses.definition: To conclude; to make something even more wonderful at the end.
senses.example: That really capped my day.

senses.definition: To shoot (someone) with a firearm.
senses.example: If he don’t get outta my hood, I’m gonna cap his ass.

senses.definition: To lie; to tell a lie.
To deprive of a cap.
To convert text to uppercase.
To take a screenshot or to record a copy of a video.
To capture an objective, such as a flag or checkpoint.
To capitulate (cause to capitulate) an opponent.
To select a player to play for a specified side.
To select to play for the national team.
senses.example: Peter Shilton is the most capped English footballer.

core.definition: A close-fitting hat, either brimless or with a peak or visor, such as a baseball cap or a knit cap.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a of cat, not the long a of cape. In fast speech the final p is often unreleased, so the word ends quickly with no puff of air.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. A cap is ordinary, casual clothing, and a person may wear one in almost any setting except formal dress occasions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cap for a baseball cap, a knit cap, or any close-fitting hat, and wear them casually in daily life. Hat is the general word, and cap suggests something smaller or sportier. In business and statistics, cap has other meanings such as a limit, but in everyday speech it almost always means headwear.

distinctions.note: Hat is the general word for any head covering, while cap usually means a closer-fitting or brimmed style, often casual or sporty.
A beanie is a knit cap with no brim, usually worn in cold weather, while a cap is the broader category.
A visor has a brim but no top covering the head, so it is not a cap, although the two are often sold together.

examples.everyday: Put on a cap before we go out, because it's really cold this morning.
examples.professional: Our team polo and cap are on the table at the check-in desk for the conference.
examples.analytical: Historians of dress read the cap as a marker of social rank, since its material and style signaled a person's place in society.

nuance.analogy: A cap is like a small roof for your head, while a hat is the whole house.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cæppe, a covering for the head, related to Late Latin cappa, a hooded cloak.
common_mistakes: Confusing cap with cape, which is a cloak; the vowel in cap is short.
Using cap for every hat, when hat is the normal general word.

cap.etymology: Inherited from Middle English *cappe*, from Old English *cæppe*, from **kappā* (“covering, hood, mantle”), from Late Latin *cappa*, itself from Latin *caput*.

senses.definition: Freight carried by a ship, aircraft, or motor vehicle.
senses.example: The plane was overloaded with cargo. It was a cargo of live animals.

senses.definition: Western material goods.
senses.example: The freighter's cargo included crates of coffee, tea, and imported machine parts.

senses.definition: To load with freight.
senses.example: The crew cargoed the barge with grain before the river froze.

core.definition: Goods or freight carried by a ship, airplane, or truck.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a clear American r and an open 'ah' vowel like 'car.' The final syllable is a long 'oh,' and the g is hard, not a 'j' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes goods in transport without emotional color.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cargo' for goods moved by ship, airplane, or truck, especially in large quantities. For ordinary shipping of goods by companies, Americans often say 'freight.' The phrase 'cargo pants,' with many pockets, is also very common in the US.

distinctions.note: Freight is goods shipped commercially, often by rail or truck, and it often refers to the shipping service as well; cargo is the goods on a particular vehicle.
Payload is a technical term for the usable cargo or load carried by an aircraft, rocket, or spacecraft, excluding fuel and crew.

examples.everyday: The truck carried a cargo of bananas down the highway to the grocery store.
examples.professional: Our team reviewed the cargo manifest before the container left the port.
examples.analytical: Histories of the Atlantic trade show how human beings were treated as cargo, a language that reveals how commerce can erase personhood.

nuance.analogy: Cargo is like the contents of a backpack, but for a vehicle large enough to carry an entire warehouse.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish cargo, 'load,' from cargar, 'to load.'
common_mistakes: Using 'cargo' as a countable noun without thinking about plural forms; 'cargoes' and 'cargos' are both used, with 'cargoes' more common in American writing.
Saying 'car-GO' with stress on the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Revelation 18:11-13 (RSV) the merchants of the earth mourn the fall of Babylon because no one buys their cargo anymore, a list of goods including gold, silver, and luxury items. The Greek word is gomos, meaning 'cargo' or 'load.' In Jonah 1:5 (RSV) the sailors throw the cargo into the sea to lighten the ship during the storm, showing cargo as the burden that must be sacrificed to survive.

cargo.etymology: Spanish *cargo* (“load, burden”), from *cargar* (“to load”), from Late Latin *carricō*.

senses.definition: The spice made from the bark of members of the genus Cinnamomum other than true cinnamon (C. verum), when they are distinguished from cinnamon.
senses.example: Add a teaspoon of cassia to the apple pie filling instead of cinnamon.

senses.definition: Such trees themselves, particularly the Chinese cinnamon, Cinnamomum cassia.
senses.example: Cassia trees line the courtyard, filling the air with a sweet, woody fragrance in spring.

senses.definition: Any of several tropical leguminous plants, of the genus Cassia.
senses.example: The pharmacist explained that cassia pods are often used in herbal laxative teas.

senses.definition: Any of several tropical leguminous plants, of the genus Senna.
senses.example: The pharmacist explained that cassia pods are often used in herbal laxative teas.

senses.definition: The sweet osmanthus (O. fragrans).
senses.example: In the garden, the cassia bloomed with tiny golden flowers that scented the whole evening.

core.definition: A spice made from the bark of a tree related to cinnamon, with a stronger, coarser flavor than true cinnamon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce ss as sh. The ending can be softened to uh in quick speech, so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized food or botanical term, mainly used in cooking, spice trade and Bible study.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans know cassia only from spice labels or from the Bible, and they usually just buy cinnamon. Cassia is common in Asian groceries and in some spice blends, and cooks sometimes notice that it is cheaper and stronger. In everyday talk, you can say cinnamon unless you are discussing the difference.

distinctions.note: Cinnamon usually means the milder true cinnamon from Ceylon, while cassia is the darker, stronger bark most often sold in American stores.
Cassia refers to the spice itself, while a cassia tree is the plant; many plants called cassia belong to a different genus, Senna.

examples.everyday: This cinnamon roll recipe calls for cassia, so the flavor will be stronger than what you're used to.
examples.professional: The spice supplier lists the product as cassia bark, not true cinnamon, so update the label before shipping.
examples.analytical: Ancient writers often used cassia and cinnamon interchangeably, which makes precise identification of biblical spices difficult.

nuance.analogy: Like a cousin of cinnamon: similar family, stronger personality.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kasia, borrowed from a Semitic source related to Hebrew qiddah.
common_mistakes: Treating cassia and cinnamon as identical, when cassia is stronger and cheaper.
Saying KASS-ee-uh; the first vowel is short and the stress falls on the first syllable with sh sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qiddah names a fragrant spice used in holy anointing oil, as in Exodus 30:24, where it is an ingredient of the sacred oil. Psalm 45:8 mentions cassia among fragrant spices in a royal wedding song. These passages show cassia as a costly aromatic used in worship and celebration.

cassia.etymology: From Latin *cassia* (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek *κασσία, κασία, κάσια*, from Hebrew *קְצִיעָה*, from Aramaic *קְצִיעֲתָא*, from *קְצַע* (“to cut off”).

senses.definition: Someone or something that catches.
senses.example: The catcher threw his mask aside and chased the runaway ball toward the backstop.

senses.definition: The player that squats behind home plate and receives the pitches from the pitcher.
The bottom partner in a homosexual relationship or sexual encounter between two men.
senses.example: The 1970s memoir described frank conversations about who played the top and who was the catcher.

core.definition: In baseball, the player who crouches behind home plate and receives the pitches thrown by the pitcher.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and end with a light American 'r' sound that is not a full 'ur' vowel. Avoid saying 'KAY-cher', since the vowel is the short /æ/ of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, 'catcher' is the everyday word for the baseball position, and fans often talk about 'the catcher' in game commentary. Outside sports, the word means a person or thing that catches something, such as a 'dust catcher'. One sexual slang sense exists in some gay male slang, but it is crude and should not be used in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: In American football, a receiver catches passes, while in baseball the catcher handles pitches behind home plate.
A goalie or goalkeeper stops shots in soccer or hockey, but a catcher is a baseball position that receives pitches.

examples.everyday: My nephew is the catcher on his Little League team, and he loves wearing the big mask.
examples.professional: We need a backup catcher for the company softball game, so can anyone in finance borrow the gear?
examples.analytical: A catcher's framing skill can shift how umpires judge borderline pitches, which makes the position more than a simple act of catching.

nuance.analogy: Like the last defender at a goal line, the catcher is the final check before the ball can pass.
nuance.etymology: From catch (verb) plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Using 'catcher' for an American football player; the usual term is 'receiver'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kuh-CHER'.

senses.definition: A group of things arranged by category.
The process of sorting or arranging things into categories or classes.

core.definition: The process of sorting or arranging things into categories or classes based on shared features.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZAY, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced to uh. The r in -ri- is pronounced, and the t is aspirated because it begins a stressed onset.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process, though in social contexts it can suggest oversimplified labeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use categorization in science, business, technology and psychology, and it is common in everyday writing about organizing information. In casual speech, people often say sorting or grouping. In American spelling it is categorization with z, not categorisation.

distinctions.note: Classification is more formal and systematic, often building hierarchies such as biological taxonomies, while categorization can be looser and more everyday.
Categorization is a neutral mental or organizational act, while stereotyping is a negative, fixed generalization about a group of people.

examples.everyday: The categorization of recipes in that app is confusing, since soups keep ending up under sides.
examples.professional: Our ticket categorization model loses accuracy whenever a request mentions two different problems.
examples.analytical: Social categorization is cognitively efficient, but it can harden into prejudice when the categories are drawn carelessly.

nuance.analogy: Like sorting a junk drawer into labeled bins, categorization is the act that turns a pile into an organized system.
nuance.etymology: From category, from Greek katēgoria, meaning predication, plus the suffix -ization.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with s (categorisation), which is British.
Stressing the first syllable instead of ZAY.

senses.definition: To discover or capture someone in the act of committing a crime.

core.definition: To be discovered in the middle of doing something wrong, especially a crime or a minor misdeed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HAN in handed, and red has a lighter secondary stress. The final -ed is a light schwa, so say the word smoothly as HAN-ded with a soft ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes someone clearly doing something wrong, though it is often said with humor about small misdeeds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use caught red-handed for serious crimes in the news and courtrooms, and also for everyday mischief, like a kid caught sneaking cookies. A natural reply in casual talk is 'Busted!' or 'Okay, you got me.' Use it in the past tense, as in 'He was caught red-handed.'

distinctions.note: Caught in the act is more neutral and literal; caught red-handed suggests the person was clearly guilty and seen in the middle of doing it.
Busted is very informal, spoken slang for being caught, often said playfully; caught red-handed works in both playful and serious contexts.

examples.everyday: My little brother got caught red-handed with frosting on his fingers and the cookie jar wide open.
examples.professional: The auditor caught the manager red-handed changing the numbers in the spreadsheet after the deadline.
examples.analytical: The prosecutor claimed the defendant was caught red-handed, but the chain of custody for the key evidence was never clearly established.

nuance.analogy: Like someone leaving the bakery with flour on their hands and a pastry in their pocket.
nuance.etymology: From the image of a person with blood still on their hands at the scene of a crime; the exact early history of the phrase is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Writing caught red handed without the hyphen; keep the hyphen in red-handed.
Using caught red-handed when no one was doing anything wrong; it always implies guilt.

conversation.text: My son was caught red-handed eating cookies before dinner.
The intern was caught red-handed changing the numbers in the spreadsheet.
The thief was caught red-handed on the store's security camera.

senses.definition: A partial obscuring of data points.
senses.example: The survival analysis handled right censoring by treating patients who left the study as partial observations.

senses.definition: An act of censorship.
senses.example: The network's censoring of the interview drew criticism from viewers who wanted the full story.

core.definition: In statistics, a data value known only partly, such as being recorded only as above or below a limit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable only, and make the middle syllable a weak r-colored schwa. The ending -ing has a short i, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical in statistics. In everyday speech it suggests suppression, so make clear you mean statistical censoring.
nuance.usage_note: In American statistics and survival analysis, people say censoring with an adjective such as right or left to specify which side of the value is unknown. Outside technical work, people use censorship for the political meaning. In a meeting, say we have censored data to avoid confusion.

distinctions.note: Censorship is the political or institutional suppression of speech or media; statistical censoring is a technical condition about incomplete measurements.
Truncation means data outside a range is never recorded at all; censoring means you know the value falls beyond a limit even if the exact value is unknown.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the survey has censoring, so some answers were cut off at the top of the scale.
examples.professional: In the churn model, customers still subscribed at the end of the study have right censoring, so we record only that their lifetime exceeds the window.
examples.analytical: Censoring forces the analyst to use likelihood methods that account for what was not observed, rather than discarding those cases or treating their endpoints as observed.

nuance.analogy: Censoring is like a race timer that stops at 10 minutes: if a runner has not finished, you know only that the time is over 10 minutes.
nuance.etymology: From censor, with the -ing suffix; the statistical sense is a later technical extension of the verb.
common_mistakes: Confusing censoring with censorship in a technical discussion, which can make a statistics explanation sound political.
Thinking right and left censoring describe the direction of the data rather than the direction of the unknown value.

senses.definition: The state of being certain.
senses.example: with certainty

senses.definition: An instance of being certain.
senses.example: Her certainty about the deadline surprised everyone, since the team still had doubts.

senses.definition: A fact or truth unquestionably established.
senses.example: That the earth orbits the sun is a certainty that no serious scientist disputes.

core.definition: The state of being completely sure that something is true, with no reasonable doubt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SUR, and the final -ty is a clear 'tee'. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so do not add an extra vowel between t and n.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, suggesting confidence and security. It can be negative when used to describe dogmatic or unjustified certainty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use certainty in both everyday and professional talk, as in 'We can't say with certainty'. In casual speech they often say 'I'm sure' instead. In professional or academic settings, certainty is a strong claim, so people typically qualify it with words like 'high confidence' or 'reasonable certainty'.

distinctions.note: Certitude is the subjective feeling of being sure, often used in religious or moral contexts, while certainty can refer to either a feeling or a well-established fact.
Confidence is trust in someone or something and is often a matter of degree, while certainty means there is no doubt.

examples.everyday: We don't have any certainty about the flight, so let's check the airline app again tomorrow morning.
examples.professional: There's no certainty that the new model will beat the baseline, so we'll run an A/B test before we ship it.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that mathematical knowledge carries a necessity and certainty that experience alone cannot supply.

nuance.analogy: Certainty is like a lighthouse on a clear night; it gives you a fixed point to steer by, but you still have to read the charts carefully.
nuance.etymology: From certain, from Latin certus, meaning fixed or determined, with the suffix -ty.
common_mistakes: Saying 'with certainty' incorrectly as 'in certainty'; the correct phrase is 'with certainty'.
Using certainty as a countable noun in the plural to mean many unrelated facts without context; it is usually uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word plerophoria, meaning full assurance or complete conviction, expresses the confident certainty that believers may have in God's promises. Hebrews 11:1 in the Revised Standard Version describes faith as the assurance of things hoped for, using the Greek word hypostasis, meaning confident grounding or substance. Hebrews 10:22 urges believers to draw near in full assurance of faith, and Hebrews 6:11 urges each believer to show the same earnestness in order to have the full assurance of hope until the end.

traditions.view: The Council of Trent taught that no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained God's grace, while Catholics may have moral certainty of God's faithfulness and hope in His promises.

Orthodox Christians usually speak of hope in God's mercy rather than a personal certainty of salvation, grounding confidence in participation in the sacraments, humility and repentance rather than in an assured inner conviction.

Reformed confessions such as the Westminster Confession teach that true believers may attain assurance of salvation, Lutherans ground assurance in the promise of the gospel, and Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants hold that assurance is real but that believers can fall away.

certainty.etymology: From Middle English *certeynte* (“surety”), from Anglo-Norman *certeinte*, from Old French *certeinete*, from Vulgar Latin **certānitās*, from Latin *certus*.

senses.definition: Resembling a chameleon: readily changing color or other attributes.
senses.example: The actor's chameleonic talent let him vanish into every role he played.

core.definition: Able to change color or adapt quickly to surroundings, moods, or situations; changing appearance easily.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AH, the fourth syllable: kuh-mee-lee-AH-nik. The first vowels are weak, and the ending is a short nik, not neek.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when praising adaptability; negative when describing someone who is fickle or insincere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chameleonic mainly in writing and thoughtful talk about people who adapt to any group or situation, sometimes to suggest they lack a firm identity. It is more literary than everyday, so in casual conversation say adaptable or flexible. It can be a compliment for an actor or negotiator, but it can sound like criticism of a politician who keeps shifting positions.

distinctions.note: Adaptable is a neutral everyday word for handling change well; chameleonic stresses a striking, almost visible shift in appearance or behavior.
Fickle means changing loyalties or interests capriciously and is usually negative; chameleonic may be admiring when it describes skill at blending in.

examples.everyday: My cousin is so chameleonic that she fits in with any group at a party.
examples.professional: Our lead designer is chameleonic, adapting her style to every client's brand without losing quality.
examples.analytical: Her chameleonic rhetoric let her speak to each audience while never committing to a single position.

nuance.analogy: Like a chameleon on a leaf, the word describes someone who takes on the color of whatever surrounds them.
nuance.etymology: From chameleon, from Greek khamaileon meaning ground lion, plus the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in kuh-MEE-lee-un-ik; the main stress is on AH.
Using it only for the literal animal; in American English it is mostly figurative.

senses.definition: One who chats or talks to excess.
senses.example: Our neighbor is a chatterbox who can talk for an hour about the weather.

senses.definition: Synonym of cootie catcher (“children's fortune-telling device”).
senses.example: At recess, my daughter showed me a chatterbox she had folded from notebook paper.

senses.definition: Synonym of chatterbot.
The orchid Epipactis gigantea.
senses.example: On our hike, the guide pointed out a chatterbox, a rare wild orchid growing in the damp shade.

core.definition: A person who talks too much, especially a talkative child or someone who chatters without stopping.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on CHAT, with a lighter secondary stress on BOX. The middle t is a flap, so it sounds like a quick 'd' and the final -er is a reduced 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or teasing; often affectionate when said to a child, but can sound irritating when said about an adult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chatterbox most often for children and close friends, usually with a smile, as in 'Oh, you little chatterbox!' Calling a colleague a chatterbox in a meeting would sound rude. Americans also use the word for a folded paper fortune-teller and for a chatbot, but in conversation the person sense comes first.

distinctions.note: Chatterbox is informal and often playful, while chatterer is more literary and less teasing.
Motormouth is slangier and more critical, suggesting someone who never stops talking.
A gossip shares rumors about other people, but a chatterbox simply talks a lot about anything.

examples.everyday: My little nephew is such a chatterbox that he tells me every detail of his day before I even take off my coat.
examples.professional: Mark is such a chatterbox in standups that we always have to cut him off to keep the meeting on time.
examples.analytical: Socrates would have called the chatterbox someone who fills the air with words without asking whether any of them are true.

nuance.analogy: A chatterbox is like a radio that never turns off, filling every silence with sound.
nuance.etymology: From chatter, of imitative origin for rapid, rattling talk, plus box; the origin of the compound is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using it for a serious adult in a formal setting, where it sounds disrespectful.
Writing the plural as 'chatterboxs' instead of 'chatterboxes.'

senses.definition: The state of being cheerful; joy.

core.definition: A positive, happy state of mind that shows in a person's manner and outlook.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the r strong. The second syllable is a reduced 'fuhl', and the final 'ness' is a weak 'nuhs'. Avoid pronouncing a full vowel in the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a pleasant, optimistic disposition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cheerfulness for a steady positive attitude, often in formal writing, reviews, or descriptions of character. In casual speech they more often say happiness or good mood. It is a formal, polished word, and you might hear it in a church, a sermon, or a letter.

distinctions.note: Happiness can describe a deep or temporary emotional state, while cheerfulness describes an outward, positive disposition.
Joy is a deeper, more intense delight, often with a spiritual or emotional depth, while cheerfulness is lighter and more everyday.

collocations: cheerfulness in the face of hardship

examples.everyday: Her cheerfulness made the long wait at the doctor's office feel shorter.
examples.professional: Her cheerfulness under pressure keeps our team calm during difficult launches.
examples.analytical: The essay distinguishes cheerfulness as a settled virtue from mere temperament, arguing that it can be cultivated through gratitude.

nuance.analogy: Cheerfulness is like a steady porch light: it is warm and welcoming, and it does not depend on the weather.
nuance.etymology: From cheerful plus the suffix '-ness'; cheer comes from Old French 'chiere', meaning face or expression.
common_mistakes: Using cheerfulness as a verb form or confusing it with cheer, which is a shout of encouragement.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a full 'ness' vowel rather than a reduced one.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word hilarotēs, meaning cheerfulness, appears in Romans 12:8, where Paul lists it among the gifts of those who show mercy. Proverbs 17:22 says that a cheerful heart is a good medicine, and that a downcast spirit dries up the bones. Both passages present cheerfulness as a sign of a healthy inner life that blesses others.

senses.definition: To pick; to make the choice of; to select.
senses.example: I chose a nice ripe apple from the fruit bowl.

senses.definition: To elect.
senses.example: He was chosen as president in 1990.

senses.definition: To decide to act in a certain way.
senses.example: I chose to walk to work today.

senses.definition: To prefer; to wish; to desire.
senses.example: You may stay for dinner if you choose, though we will understand if you're busy.

senses.definition: The binomial coefficient of the previous and following number.
senses.example: The number of distinct subsets of size k from a set of size n is (nk) or "n choose k".

core.definition: To pick one or more things from several options, based on what you prefer or need.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long oo vowel and end with a clean z sound. Do not add a y sound or a separate syllable, and keep it distinct from 'chose' /tʃoʊz/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an everyday or formal decision, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use choose for everyday decisions, such as picking food, a plan or a candidate, and it fits both casual and formal situations. For quick everyday picks, many Americans say pick. In a formal document or election, choose may be replaced by elect or select. Note that the past tense is 'chose' and the past participle is 'chosen'.

distinctions.note: Pick is more casual and everyday, while choose is neutral and can carry more weight in decisions.
Select is more formal and is common in business, technology and menus.
Elect specifically means choose by vote, typically for an office.

examples.everyday: You can choose any dessert you like, and I will pay for it.
examples.professional: We need to choose one vendor by Friday so legal can review the contract.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that a rational agent cannot choose an end without accepting the principle that makes it binding.

nuance.analogy: Like a shopper standing before two shirts, hand hovering until one is picked.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cēosan, meaning to select or prefer.
common_mistakes: Using 'choose' with a bare infinitive or gerund incorrectly, as in 'I choose going' instead of 'I choose to go'.
Writing 'choosed' or 'have choose' instead of 'chose' and 'have chosen'.
Using 'between' for more than two options, where 'among' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The English 'choose' translates Hebrew bahar and Greek eklegomai, both meaning to pick out or select. The Bible uses it of God choosing Israel, of God choosing believers and of people choosing how to live. Deuteronomy 7:6 says the LORD chose Israel to be a people for his own possession. John 15:16 has Jesus saying that the disciples did not choose him, but he chose them. Joshua 24:15 has Joshua urging the people to choose whom they will serve.

choose.etymology: From Middle English *chesen*, from Old English *ċēosan* (“to choose, seek out, select, elect, decide, test, accept, settle for, approve”), from **keusan*, from Proto-Germanic **keusaną* (“to test; to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European **ǵéwseti* (“to…

senses.definition: The branch of Christian theology concerned with the person, natures and work of Jesus Christ.
senses.example: Our seminary course on Christology examined how the early councils defined Christ's divine and human natures.

senses.definition: A particular account or understanding of Christ, as held by a writer, text or tradition.
senses.example: Her essay criticizes the Christology of the Gospel of John as too focused on divinity.

core.definition: The part of theology that studies who Jesus Christ is, especially how he is both God and man; also a particular view of this.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAH, the second syllable, as in biology. The 'Ch' is a hard 'k', and the first vowel is short 'ih', not 'Christ' with a long 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a standard academic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Christology in seminaries, sermons that teach doctrine and biblical scholarship. Scholars speak of 'high Christology' (stressing Christ's divinity) and 'low Christology' (beginning from his humanity), and of the Christology of a particular Gospel. It is capitalized because it comes from Christ.

distinctions.note: Soteriology is the doctrine of salvation; Christology is the doctrine of the person of Christ, though the two are closely linked.
Christocentric describes theology or preaching that centers on Christ; Christology is the study itself.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study is reading John this fall, and the leader keeps pointing out how high its Christology is.
examples.professional: The doctoral seminar on early Christology starts with Paul's letters and ends with the Council of Chalcedon.
examples.analytical: Every Christology must explain how one subject can both suffer on the cross and be the eternal Son without denying either claim.

nuance.etymology: From Greek Christos 'anointed one' (translating Hebrew mashiach, 'Messiah') and -logia 'study, account'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'KRIES-tology' with the vowel of Christ; Americans say krih-STAH-luh-jee.
Writing it with a lowercase c.
nuance.biblical_note: The word is not in Scripture, but the New Testament supplies its material. The prologue of John presents the Word who was with God, was God and became flesh (John 1:1-14). Philippians 2:5-11 describes Christ, who was in the form of God, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant. Colossians 1:15-20 calls him the image of the invisible God in whom all things hold together.

senses.definition: The state of being circuitous.

core.definition: The quality of taking a long, winding, indirect route instead of the most direct one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KYOO, the second syllable, and the remaining syllables are all reduced to weak vowels. Don't say sir-kwi-TOO-ness with the stress on the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral: it suggests unnecessary delay or confusion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use circuitousness in conversation; they say a roundabout way, winding or a long way around. The noun appears in formal writing, policy discussions and literary criticism. In speech, you might say 'The route was so roundabout' and save the noun for careful writing.

distinctions.note: Indirectness describes a way of speaking or acting that avoids saying things plainly; circuitousness describes a path, process or argument that takes extra steps.
Wordiness means using too many words; circuitousness means taking too many steps, though an argument can have both.

examples.professional: The approval process has so much circuitousness that a simple form can take three months to sign.
examples.analytical: The circuitousness of his argument obscures a claim that could have been made in a single sentence.

nuance.analogy: Circuitousness is like a hiking trail that loops around a mountain when a straight path up the side was available.
