senses.definition: The complete body of government ministers (whether or not they are in cabinet) under the leadership of a head of government (such as a prime minister)
senses.example: The premier offered his last ministry's resignation to the monarch, and is asked to form a new one in accordance with the election results.

senses.definition: A ministration.
senses.example: The nurse's quiet ministry at the bedside comforted the dying man's family.

senses.definition: The active practice and education of the minister of a particular religion or faith.
senses.example: She enrolled in seminary to pursue ministry after years working as an accountant.

senses.definition: The clergy of nonapostolic Protestant churches.
senses.example: The church's ministry gathered for the ordination of three new pastors.

senses.definition: Work of a spiritual or charitable nature.
senses.example: the present ministry of the Holy Spirit

core.definition: Work or service performed in a church, such as preaching, pastoral care, or a specific outreach program.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final 'ry' is pronounced like 'ree,' and the middle 'is' is a reduced 'uh' sound, not 'eye.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful in church settings. In government contexts it is neutral, and in general use it is more formal.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, ministry commonly refers to a specific program, such as 'the youth ministry' or 'the prison ministry,' or to a church's overall service. Americans sometimes say 'a ministry' for a faith-based organization, and they also use the word for a pastor's calling, as in 'entering the ministry.' For government departments, Americans say 'department' or 'agency,' and 'ministry' is mainly used for other countries.

distinctions.note: In American government, department is the normal term for a unit of the executive branch, while ministry refers to the equivalent unit in other countries.

examples.everyday: My sister joined the food pantry ministry at her church, and she spends Saturday mornings packing boxes for families.
examples.professional: The church's outreach ministry is hiring a coordinator to manage volunteers and our community partnerships.
examples.analytical: Paul describes the church as a body in which each member has a ministry, arguing that all gifts serve the common good.

nuance.analogy: A ministry is like the crew on a ship: each person has a particular job, but all of them move the vessel toward the same destination.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin ministerium, 'service, office,' from minister, 'servant.'
common_mistakes: Using 'ministry' for a U.S. government department, when Americans say 'department' or 'agency.'
Saying 'ministry' to mean only a pastor's job, when it can refer to any church service or program.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is diakonia, 'service, ministry,' and the RSV uses 'ministry' for it in several passages. In Acts 6:4, the apostles say they will devote themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. In Ephesians 4:12, the RSV says the gifts of Christ are given for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry.

traditions.view: Ministry is understood mainly as the sacramental service of ordained clergy, though all baptized members share in the church's common life and witness.
Ministry includes the ordained ministries of bishop, priest, and deacon, and also the wider service of the laity, who take part in the Church's mission in many ways.
Many Protestants teach the priesthood of all believers, so ministry belongs to all Christians, while some churches also recognize a set-apart office of pastors and elders.

ministry.etymology: From Middle English *mynisterie*, borrowed from Old French *menistere*, in turn borrowed itself from Latin *ministerium*; equivalent to *minister* + *-y*.

senses.definition: The property of being miserly: excessive parsimony.

core.definition: The quality of being miserly; an excessive unwillingness to spend money or share what you have.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MY, not on 'mis'. The middle syllable -er- is a quick, r-colored schwa, and the ending -ness is a reduced 'nus'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for hoarding money or refusing to spend, and it is usually said with disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'miserliness' in both conversation and writing, though 'stinginess' is more common in everyday talk. Calling someone's behavior 'miserliness' sounds somewhat formal and can be a sharp criticism. In casual conversation, Americans often say someone is 'cheap' or 'stingy' instead.

distinctions.note: Stinginess is the everyday word and can be mild, while miserliness is stronger and suggests an obsessive habit of hoarding.
Thrift means careful, sensible saving and is a positive quality, while miserliness is excessive and usually disapproved of.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's miserliness is famous; he won't even buy a lawn mower and borrows ours every summer.
examples.professional: Her team's miserliness with the training budget means we keep losing good engineers to competitors.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats miserliness as a vice opposed to liberality, a fault of getting and keeping wealth that never leads to giving.

nuance.analogy: Like a squirrel that hides so many nuts it forgets to eat, miserliness keeps its treasure so tightly that it loses the point of having it.
nuance.etymology: From 'miserly' (miser plus -ly) plus the suffix -ness; 'miser' comes from Latin miser, wretched.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'miserliness' with 'miserableness'; the first means stinginess, the second means unhappiness.
Putting the stress on the second syllable instead of the first, MY-zer-lin-us.

core.definition: Hostile to change and dismissive of new ideas or innovations.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on IS, the fourth syllable, and the final -tik is short and light. Do not stress the earlier syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes resistance to progress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use misoneistic mainly in essays, history, or philosophy. In everyday speech, say someone is against change or will not try anything new. Like misoneist, it can sound stiff in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Conservative describes a general preference for tradition, not hostility to new ideas.
Reactionary describes political opposition to progressive change and carries a stronger political sense.

examples.everyday: My uncle is still pretty misoneistic about new gadgets, but he is slowly warming up.
examples.professional: The board's misoneistic response to the proposal delayed the pilot by a full year.
examples.analytical: Many nineteenth-century critics held a misoneistic view of the new science, fearing it would unsettle religious and social order.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who keeps pulling up every new shoot.
nuance.etymology: From misoneism, from Greek miso- meaning hatred and neos meaning new, with the suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a noun; misoneistic is an adjective, and misoneist is the noun.
Putting the main stress on the early syllables instead of IS.

senses.definition: To understand wrongly, taking one thing or person for another.
senses.example: Sorry, I mistook you for my brother. You look very similar.

senses.definition: An error.
senses.example: There were too many mistakes in the test that, unfortunately, made you fail.

senses.definition: A pitch which was intended to be pitched in a hard-to-hit location, but instead ends up in an easy-to-hit place.
senses.example: The pitcher's mistake was a fastball that drifted belt-high over the middle of the plate.

core.definition: An error, or something done wrongly by accident or through poor judgment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STAYK. The first syllable is weak, so keep it short and reduced. The k at the end should be clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it ranges from a trivial slip to a serious error, and is often said with an apology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mistake' constantly, for everything from a wrong number to a serious error. The phrase 'by mistake' is very common in everyday speech. A typical reply to an apology is 'No worries, it happens' or 'That's okay, everybody makes mistakes.'

distinctions.note: Error is more formal and is used in technical or official contexts, while mistake is everyday language.
A mix-up is confusion between two things or people, while a mistake is any wrong act or result.
An oversight is a mistake from failing to notice something, and it suggests carelessness about what should have been caught.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I made a mistake and sent you the wrong file.
examples.professional: We made a mistake in the cost estimate, so I'm sending a corrected spreadsheet this afternoon.
examples.analytical: A mistake in reasoning differs from a moral failure, because an agent may follow the rules and still draw a false conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A mistake is like a wrong turn on a road trip: you notice, you turn around, and you keep going.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English mistaken, from Old Norse mistaka, 'to take in error'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I did a mistake'; the usual phrase is 'I made a mistake'.
Saying 'in mistake' instead of 'by mistake'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word shegagah means an unintentional error or sin of inadvertence. Leviticus 4:2 describes a person who sins unintentionally and must bring a sin offering. Numbers 15:27-29 gives similar provision for unintentional sins, and the Greek hamartia, 'missing the mark', also carries the sense of sin as error.

mistake.etymology: From Middle English *mistaken*, from Old Norse *mistaka* (“to take in error, to miscarry”); equivalent to *mis* + *take*.

senses.definition: Synonym of cure.
senses.example: The old physician swore his mithridate was a sure cure for every poison in the realm.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of mithridate mustard.
(historical) Any of various historical medicines, typically an electuary compounded with various poison, believed to derive from Mithridates VI and to serve as a universal antidote.
senses.example: Renaissance apothecaries sold expensive mithridate to nobles who feared being poisoned at dinner.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A historical medicine, usually a compound paste, once believed to be an antidote that protected against all poisons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the th is voiceless as in think. The final syllable is a clear -dayt, not -dut, and the middle syllable is reduced to a quick uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical term, with no modern positive or negative connotation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside the history of medicine, classical literature, or pharmacy history. In modern English, say antidote or universal antidote. You are most likely to meet it in historical texts or literary references.

distinctions.note: Antidote is the modern general term for a substance that counters a poison; mithridate is a specific historical compound claimed to work against all poisons.
Theriac was a related historical compound medicine of similar purpose, so writers sometimes mention both together.

examples.everyday: He jokes that years of my cooking have made him immune, like someone who lived on a mithridate.
examples.professional: In the history of medicine seminar, we compared the mithridate with the pharmacopeias of later centuries.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers presented the mithridate as the emblem of a universal remedy, a promise that one compound could neutralize every known poison.

nuance.analogy: A medieval cure-all that promised protection against any poison, like a castle built to withstand every siege.
nuance.etymology: From Mithridates VI of Pontus, the king said to have tried to make himself immune to poison.
common_mistakes: Confusing mithridate (the medicine) with mithridatism (the gradual building of immunity).
Using mithridate as a modern word for antidote in everyday English.

mithridate.etymology: From Middle English *mitridate* and *methridat*, from Old French *mithridat*, from Late Latin *mithridatum* and *mithridatium*, from Latin *Mithridātīus* (“of or related to Mithridates”), from *Mithridātēs* + *-ius*, from Ancient Greek *Μιθριδάτης*, the…

senses.definition: Any of various long-tailed American songbirds of the genera Mimus and Melanotis, noted for their ability to mimic calls of other birds.
senses.example: A northern mockingbird sang a medley of car alarms and blue jay calls outside my window.

senses.definition: Synonym of tui (“a species of honeyeater, Prosthemadera novaeseelandiae, a bird which is endemic to New Zealand”).
senses.example: In New Zealand, locals call the tui a mockingbird because of its varied, mimicking song.

core.definition: A gray American songbird known for copying the calls and songs of other birds and even mechanical sounds.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MAH, the first syllable. The middle vowel is the short 'ih' of 'sit', so 'king' has the reduced vowel not the long 'ing' sound. The final -bird is rhotic with an American 'r' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. In American culture it often symbolizes innocence, especially after Harper Lee's novel To Kill a Mockingbird.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mockingbird for the bird that copies sounds, often heard singing at night in gardens and cities across the South. The word is also a cultural symbol because of To Kill a Mockingbird, where killing one is treated as a sin against innocence. Do not confuse the bird's name with the verb 'mock'; the bird does not mock but imitates.

distinctions.note: A parrot imitates speech, while a mockingbird imitates a wide range of sounds, including other birds' songs and car alarms.
Songbird is a broad category for birds that sing; mockingbird names one specific species famous for mimicry.
A catbird is a different American bird that mews like a cat; it is also a mimic, but it is not a mockingbird.

collocations: a mockingbird in the magnolia tree

examples.everyday: Every spring a mockingbird sits on our fence and copies the sound of our car alarm, which drives the dog crazy.
examples.professional: The park conservancy logged a mockingbird nesting near the trail, so we rescheduled the tree trimming.
examples.analytical: Lee's title turns the mockingbird into a moral emblem: the innocent who harms no one and deserves protection.

nuance.analogy: A mockingbird is like a gifted impressionist who can copy any voice in the room, though the voices belong to someone else.
nuance.etymology: From mock (imitate) and bird; the name refers to the bird's habit of imitating other birds' calls.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a long 'ing', as in 'MAH-keeng'; it is a short, reduced vowel.
Thinking the bird mocks people in an unkind way; its name describes mimicry, not ridicule.

mockingbird.etymology: From *mocking* + *bird*, from the ability of the birds to mimic sounds and, in some cases, hum as a wake-up call.

senses.definition: Said, written, or done with the intent to mock, or ridicule; with mocking effect.
senses.example: She repeated his promise mockingly, then laughed when he flushed and looked away.

core.definition: In a way that teases or makes fun of someone or something, often in a scornful or playful tone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH. The second vowel is short and reduced, so 'king' sounds like 'kihng' with a weak vowel. The final -ly is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It shows scorn, teasing or ridicule, though it can be playful in friendly contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mockingly to describe a tone of voice or a gesture when someone is making fun of another person or idea. It is common in everyday speech and writing, especially in stories and reviews. It often appears with verbs like say, smile, bow or repeat, and it can be used lightly among friends.

distinctions.note: Teasingly is usually friendly and playful, while mockingly often implies scorn or ridicule.
Sarcastically means saying the opposite of what you mean; mockingly can imitate or exaggerate someone else's words without the same irony.
Jokingly means as a joke with no real malice; mockingly has a sharper, more critical edge.

examples.everyday: 'Oh, great,' she said mockingly when I dropped the milk again.
examples.professional: He mockingly thanked the team for finally hitting the deadline, which made it clear he had not expected us to succeed.
examples.analytical: Pope presents the vain fop mockingly, treating his trivial vanity with the solemn weight of an epic hero.

nuance.analogy: Like a comedian's imitation of a politician: the voice is copied exactly, but the point is to make the listener laugh at it.
nuance.etymology: From mocking (present participle of mock) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing mockingly with 'mockingbird' or using it as a noun; it is an adverb only.
Using mockingly for kindly teasing between close friends, which may sound too harsh.

senses.definition: The act or process of shaping in or on a mold, or of making molds; the art or occupation of a molder.
senses.example: Molding the aluminum parts takes careful temperature control on our factory floor.

senses.definition: Anything cast in a mold, or which appears to be so, as grooved or ornamental bars of wood or metal.
senses.example: The crown molding along the ceiling was carved from solid oak by hand.

senses.definition: A planing machine for making moldings.
senses.example: The shop's molding machine shapes the trim boards in a single pass.

senses.definition: A machine to assist in making molds for castings.
senses.example: The foundry bought a new molding machine to speed up casting production.

senses.definition: A mill for shaping timber.
senses.example: The sawmill's molding mill shapes rough planks into decorative trim for furniture.

senses.definition: A kind of sand containing clay, used in making molds.
senses.example: The foundry packed the flask with molding sand mixed with clay and water.

senses.definition: A plane, or curved, narrow surface, either sunk or projecting, used for decoration by means of the lights and shades upon its surface and to conceal joints, especially between unlike materials.
senses.example: The carpenter added a molding along the top of the cabinet to hide the seam.

core.definition: A decorative strip of wood, plaster, or metal used to trim walls, ceilings, or doorways, or the process of shaping material in a mold.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ol' sounds like 'ohl' and the 'ding' ends with a nasal 'ng,' so do not add an extra vowel between 'l' and 'd.' Keep it to two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a building or craft element without strong emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American home improvement and construction talk, 'molding' is common: 'crown molding,' 'baseboard molding,' and 'door molding.' Americans also use 'trim' as a general word for finishing woodwork. The American spelling is 'molding'; British 'moulding' should not be used in American writing.

distinctions.note: 'Trim' is a broader term for finishing woodwork around doors and windows; 'molding' specifically means a shaped profile.
A 'mold' is a hollow form used to shape material; 'molding' is the decorative piece or the act of shaping.

examples.everyday: We're putting new crown molding in the living room, so the ceiling will look much more finished.
examples.professional: The contractor will install the baseboard molding after the drywall dries, so the joints stay tight.
examples.analytical: The architect's molding profiles recall classical cornice designs, and the essay reads them as a visual argument about authority.

nuance.analogy: Molding is like the frame around a painting: it does not change the picture, but it finishes the edge and hides the seam.
nuance.etymology: From mold (Old French modle, from Latin modulus 'small measure') plus -ing; the decorative sense developed from the shaped profile.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'moulding' in American writing.
Confusing 'molding' (trim) with 'mold' (a hollow form or fungus).

senses.definition: Melted, especially due to great heat.
senses.example: molten metal, wax, rock

senses.definition: Made from a melted substance. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The foundry crew poured molten iron into the sand molds at dawn.

senses.definition: Glowing red-hot.
senses.example: The horseshoe glowed molten red in the blacksmith's fire.

core.definition: Melted by very high heat and turned into a hot liquid, such as molten metal or molten lava.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOHL. The second syllable is reduced to a soft 'tun', like 'button' without the t sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to vivid. It describes something extremely hot and liquid, often with a sense of power or danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use molten mainly for metals, rock, glass, and food when it is extremely hot, such as molten chocolate cake or molten cheese. It is used before a noun, as in 'molten steel.' It is less common for ordinary melted butter, where people usually say melted.

distinctions.note: Melted is the everyday word for anything that has turned liquid, while molten emphasizes intense heat and usually appears before a noun.
Liquid is a general state of matter, while molten describes a substance that is liquid because it has been heated to a high temperature.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that dessert, the chocolate inside is molten and will burn your mouth.
examples.professional: The foundry crew poured molten steel into the molds before dawn.
examples.analytical: Scientists propose that Earth's outer core is molten, which helps generate the planet's magnetic field.

nuance.analogy: Molten is like candle wax at the point where it has turned into a hot, flowing pool.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of melt, from Old English meltan; the form molten is an older past participle kept in set uses.
common_mistakes: Using molten for any melted substance, such as melted butter, where melted is more natural.
Placing molten after the noun, as in 'the metal molten' instead of 'molten metal'.
Pronouncing it as 'MOL-ten' with a short vowel.

molten.etymology: From Middle English *molten*, from Old English *molten*, *ġemolten* (“melted, molten”), from Proto-Germanic **multanaz*, past participle of Proto-Germanic **meltaną* (“to melt”).

senses.definition: A Christian position holding that God, through the Holy Spirit, works to bring about effectually the salvation of individuals through spiritual regeneration without cooperation from the individual.

core.definition: The Christian teaching that God alone, by the Holy Spirit, accomplishes a person's regeneration and salvation without human cooperation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, which has the 'ah' vowel of 'father'. The g is a J sound, not a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a technical term; positive among Reformed believers, and often disputed by others.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theological discussion, especially among Reformed and Lutheran Christians. It is usually contrasted with synergism. Most Americans outside theology circles will not know the word.

distinctions.note: Synergism holds that God and the human will cooperate in salvation, while monergism says God alone acts in regeneration.
Predestination concerns God's choice of people, while monergism concerns how salvation is worked in them.
Calvinism is a broader system that includes monergism, but monergism is a narrower claim about the working of grace.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we argued about monergism and whether we really choose God.
examples.professional: The lecture outlines monergism and synergism as two models of how grace operates in conversion.
examples.analytical: Monergism safeguards the claim that salvation is wholly God's gift, but it raises hard questions about human responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Monergism is like a rescuer pulling a drowning person from the water, rather than a swimmer who helps by paddling.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monos, 'alone, single', and ergon, 'work'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g as in 'go'.
Confusing it with 'monism'.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Advocates cite Ephesians 2:8-9, which says salvation is by grace through faith and not our own doing, and John 6:44, where no one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws them. Ezekiel 36:26-27 speaks of God giving a new heart and spirit.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy generally teaches synergy, in which human freedom cooperates with divine grace, and so does not accept monergism as defined in the West.
Catholicism teaches that grace comes first and is necessary, but that the human will freely cooperates with it, so it is generally described as synergistic.

Lutheran and Reformed Christians typically affirm that God alone brings about conversion, though they differ on election and resistibility of grace. Arminian, Wesleyan, and many Baptist and Pentecostal Christians hold that grace enables but does not override free response.

senses.definition: A proponent of monergism.

core.definition: A person who holds monergism, the doctrine that God alone works the new birth and salvation without human cooperation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH-. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored vowel, and the 'g' is pronounced like the 'j' in judge, so the word sounds like MAH-nur-jist, not mon-er-GIST.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, though used in theological debate it can signal a sharp doctrinal position.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in theology, seminary classrooms, and church debates about salvation, especially among Reformed and Calvinist Christians. In everyday church talk, people more often say Calvinist or Reformed. Use it when stating a position precisely, since opponents sometimes use it as a label too.

distinctions.note: A synergist holds that God and the human will cooperate in conversion, while a monergist holds that God alone effects it.
Calvinist is a broader label for followers of Calvin's theology, and monergism is one doctrine within it.
An Arminian holds that prevenient grace enables a free human response, which a monergist rejects as a cooperative view of regeneration.

examples.everyday: At Bible study, one guy said he's a monergist, meaning God does the whole work of salvation, and we spent an hour on it.
examples.professional: The seminary course on soteriology compares monergist and synergist accounts of regeneration.
examples.analytical: A monergist argues that regeneration precedes faith, so the human will cannot be the cause of the new birth.

nuance.analogy: A monergist sees God as the only author of a rescue, not a lifeguard who needs the drowning person to swim toward him.
nuance.etymology: From Greek monos 'alone' and ergon 'work', so 'work done by one alone'.
common_mistakes: Confusing monergism with monotheism, which is belief in one God
Stressing the second syllable, saying mon-er-JIST
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself is a theological label not found in Scripture. Its Greek root is ergon, meaning work or deed. Ephesians 2:8-9 describes salvation as God's gift received through faith rather than from works, which monergists read as God's sole agency. Philippians 1:6 says God who began a good work will bring it to completion, which monergists cite for God's sustaining work. Philippians 2:12-13 tells believers to work out their salvation because God is at work in them, which synergists read as cooperation and monergists read as God's own energy producing both will and action.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy speaks of synergy, the cooperation of God's grace with the free response of the person, and generally rejects monergism as failing to respect human freedom in salvation.

Catholic teaching holds that grace precedes and enables the human will, which then freely cooperates, as affirmed at the Council of Trent. Catholics affirm God as the primary cause of salvation but generally reject pure monergism.

Reformed and Calvinist Protestants hold monergism, that God alone regenerates the sinner and faith is his gift. Lutherans teach that the Spirit alone converts and reject synergism in conversion, while Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants reject monergism in favor of prevenient grace that enables a free response.

senses.definition: An injective homomorphism.
senses.example: The map from the subgroup into the larger group is a monomorphism, so its kernel is trivial.

senses.definition: A morphism n such that for any other morphisms f and g, if n∘f=n∘g then f = g.
senses.example: Show that n is a monomorphism by checking that n∘f = n∘g forces f = g.

senses.definition: The absence of sexual dimorphism.
senses.example: Biologists noted the lizards' monomorphism, since males and females look nearly identical.

core.definition: In algebra, a one-to-one structure-preserving map; in category theory, a morphism that can be canceled on the left.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MOR, and the first syllable keeps a secondary stress. The ending -ism is reduced to a weak 'um' sound, not a full 'eyes-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists use this word in algebra, category theory and type theory. Outside those fields it is almost never used. In algebra the word is often used as a synonym for injective homomorphism, while in category theory it has a more general definition. Always check which definition the context assumes.

distinctions.note: A monomorphism is cancellable on the left, while an epimorphism is cancellable on the right, so the two are dual concepts.
An injective map is a set-level term, while monomorphism is the category-theoretic generalization that does not require elements.

examples.everyday: I could not follow my nephew when he started explaining monomorphism at dinner, so I just nodded.
examples.professional: Before we merge the two modules, we should confirm that the mapping is a monomorphism so no information gets lost.
examples.analytical: A morphism is a monomorphism precisely when it can be canceled on the left, which in concrete categories often amounts to injectivity.

nuance.analogy: Think of a monomorphism as a one-way filter that never lets two different inputs collapse into the same output, so you can always trace back where something came from.
nuance.etymology: From mono- (single) and Greek morphē (form), with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing monomorphism with monomorphic, the adjective, which is used in computing for a different sense.
Stressing the final syllable, as in mon-oh-mor-FIZ-um.

senses.definition: The sloping side of a mountain.

core.definition: The sloping surface or side of a mountain, from the base to the top.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced, nearly silent 'tun'. The final 'side' has the diphthong 'ai' as in 'ride'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place or a surface and carries a mild sense of scenery or outdoor life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mountainside' in everyday talk about hiking, scenery, or a house built on a slope. It is more common in speech than 'slope of a mountain'. People also say 'hillside' for a smaller hill, and 'the side of the mountain' is a natural alternative.

distinctions.note: A hillside is on a smaller, lower elevation, while a mountainside belongs to a larger, steeper mountain.
A slope is any inclined surface, while a mountainside is specifically the side of a mountain.

examples.everyday: We hiked up the mountainside and stopped to look at the lake far below.
examples.professional: The survey crew mapped erosion along the mountainside after the spring storms.
examples.analytical: The poem imagines the mountainside as a place where human speech and divine speech meet.

nuance.analogy: Like the sloping side of a tent, which rises from the ground up to the peak.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'mountain' and 'side', from Old French montaigne and Old English sīde.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'mountain side', in formal writing; the standard spelling is one word.
Using 'on the mountainside' versus 'in the mountainside' inconsistently; 'on' is the usual preposition for a surface.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word for mountain is 'har', and mountains in Scripture are often places of revelation, prayer, and teaching. Matthew 5:1 describes Jesus going up onto a mountain before he teaches the crowds. Mark 3:13 describes Jesus going up on the mountain to call the twelve apostles. Matthew 28:16 says the eleven disciples went to the mountain where Jesus had told them to meet him.

senses.definition: Unbiased trade between nations, in contrast to bilateralism.
senses.example: Economists debated whether multilateralism in trade would serve developing nations better than bilateral deals.

senses.definition: A system by which nations consult others in matters of foreign policy, by way of organizations such as the United Nations.
senses.example: Her speech defended multilateralism, arguing that allies should consult one another through the United Nations before acting.

core.definition: A policy of cooperation among three or more countries, typically through organizations like the United Nations, rather than only through pairs of nations.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAT, and the t in multilateral is a flap that sounds close to a soft d. The final -ism is reduced to a short uhm.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in diplomacy. Supporters praise it as stable and rule-based, while critics call it slow or a limit on national sovereignty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news about foreign policy, the United Nations, NATO, and trade agreements, and in political debates. It is formal and rarely appears in casual conversation. In everyday talk, people would say 'working with allies' or 'going through the UN.' The opposite is unilateralism, acting alone.

distinctions.note: Bilateralism involves agreements between two countries, while multilateralism involves three or more.
Internationalism is a broader attitude favoring global cooperation, while multilateralism is a specific method of acting through many-country arrangements.
Unilateralism means acting alone without consulting others, which is the opposite of multilateralism.

examples.everyday: At dinner, my dad argued that multilateralism works better than going it alone, and my sister disagreed.
examples.professional: Our trade compliance team tracks how multilateralism shapes the rules for export controls.
examples.analytical: Multilateralism rests on the assumption that shared rules constrain power, which is precisely why powerful states sometimes resist it.

nuance.analogy: A group chat with agreed house rules, instead of a set of private texts between each pair of people.
nuance.etymology: From multilateral plus -ism; multilateral comes from multi- (many) and lateral, from Latin latus, side.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with multilingualism or multinational; it refers to arrangements among several countries, not languages or companies.
Stressing the final syllable instead of LAT, or pronouncing the t as a hard t rather than a flap.

senses.definition: Supporting or advocating multilateralism.
senses.example: The senator gave a multilateralist speech urging allies to coordinate sanctions together.

senses.definition: An advocate of multilateralism.
senses.example: She has been a committed multilateralist since her years at the State Department.

core.definition: A person who favors cooperation among several countries through international organizations, rather than acting alone or only in pairs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAT, and make the t a quick flap that sounds like a soft d. The final -ist is a short, clear syllable, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, depending on who uses it. Supporters see a multilateralist as principled, while critics may call the same person naive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in political news and foreign policy discussions, often for people who favor working through the UN, NATO, and treaties. Calling someone a multilateralist is neutral or positive, and it sounds formal. You would rarely use it in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Internationalist is broader and can describe any global outlook, while multilateralist refers specifically to preferring many-country agreements and institutions.
Globalist is often a loaded political term used by critics, while multilateralist sounds more technical and policy-focused.

examples.professional: As a multilateralist, she pushed the company to join the industry standards body instead of building its own protocol.
examples.analytical: The multilateralist tradition assumes that institutions can restrain the self-interest of states, a claim that realists dispute.

nuance.analogy: Someone who prefers a committee decision to a solo verdict.
nuance.etymology: From multilateralism plus the suffix -ist, a person who holds or practices a belief.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for multinational; a multilateralist supports cooperation among countries, not among companies.
Pronouncing the t as a hard t instead of a flap, or stressing the final syllable.

senses.definition: Polynomial.
senses.example: Expanding the multinomial (x + y)^3 by hand is a useful exercise in algebra.

senses.definition: Polynomial.
senses.example: Expanding the multinomial (x + y)^3 by hand is a useful exercise in algebra.

core.definition: In statistics, describing a distribution or model with more than two possible outcomes per trial, generalizing the binomial.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NOH, the third-syllable-ish main stress, with the first syllable secondary. The ending '-ial' is reduced to 'ee-ul', and the i in 'multi' is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise statistical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use multinomial almost only in statistics, machine learning and math courses. The common phrase is multinomial logistic regression for classification with several categories. In everyday speech, people say 'with several categories' or 'with many outcomes'.

distinctions.note: Binomial has exactly two outcomes per trial; multinomial allows three or more.
In algebra, a multinomial is a polynomial with more than one term, but in statistics the term refers to a distribution over several categories.

examples.everyday: My sister studies stats and keeps saying multinomial, which is just a fancy way of saying many categories.
examples.professional: For the survey data with five response options, a multinomial logistic regression is the right choice.
examples.analytical: Under a multinomial model, the probabilities of all categories sum to one, which constrains the parameters jointly.

nuance.analogy: Like rolling a die with six faces instead of flipping a coin with two.
nuance.etymology: Coined on binomial (Latin bi-, two, plus nomen, name or term), with multi- (many) replacing bi-.
common_mistakes: Using multinomial to mean any polynomial in everyday talk; in statistics it means several outcome categories.
Putting the main stress on the wrong syllable; say mul-tee-NOH-mee-ul.

senses.definition: Resembling or having the consistency of mush; semiliquid, pasty, or granular.
senses.example: I don't especially like mushy oatmeal.

senses.definition: Soft; squishy.
senses.example: The brake pedal is mushy sometimes when I step on it.

senses.definition: Overly sappy, corny, or cheesy; sentimental, especially in a romantic way; maudlin.
senses.example: Skip the mushy, romantic scenes and get to the action.

core.definition: Soft, pulpy, and squishy, like overcooked food or fruit that has lost its firmness.

pronunciation.tip: The first vowel is short and relaxed, like the 'u' in 'cut', not 'oo'. The sh is followed by a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative for food, since it suggests poor texture. Negative or teasing for sentimental romance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mushy for overcooked vegetables, bananas that are too ripe, or cereal that has soaked too long. In informal speech it also describes sappy romantic movies or emotional talk, often with a teasing tone. Saying something is too mushy is mildly critical and casual.

distinctions.note: Soggy means soaked with liquid. Mushy means soft and pulpy, even without much water.
Squishy suggests something soft that gives under pressure. Mushy suggests a broken-down, pasty texture.

examples.everyday: The bananas got too mushy, so I made them into bread.
examples.professional: The slides were mushy with too many words, so let's simplify them before the review.
examples.analytical: The author's argument is mushy because it avoids committing to any clear definition.

nuance.analogy: Like bread left too long in soup, losing its shape completely.
nuance.etymology: Formed from mush, a soft mass of food, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel like 'oo' (MOO-shee).
Using mushy for liquid soup; it describes soft solid texture.

conversation.text: The vegetables were overcooked and mushy.
I don't like mushy bananas, so I eat them a little green.
The pasta got mushy because I boiled it too long.

senses.definition: Shrinking.
senses.example: The narrowing road forced drivers to slow down before the old stone bridge.

senses.definition: The process of becoming narrow.
senses.example: narrowings of the road

senses.definition: The part of a stocking that is narrowed.
senses.example: She knitted the heel carefully, then worked the narrowing before starting the foot.

core.definition: The process of becoming narrower, or a place where something has become narrower.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NAR, and make the final syllable a quick 'ing' with no extra vowel. Pronounce the r clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a change in size or scope, and it can be positive or negative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use narrowing in medicine, engineering and everyday speech, as in 'a narrowing of the artery' or 'a narrowing of the gap'. In casual talk, people often say 'getting narrower' instead. It can also describe a shrinking set of options or topics.

distinctions.note: Narrowness is the state of being narrow; narrowing is the process or result of becoming narrower.
Constriction is a tightening that squeezes or restricts something, often in medicine; narrowing is a more general reduction in width.

examples.everyday: The doctor said there is a narrowing in one of my arteries, so I need to watch my diet.
examples.professional: The narrowing of the search window cut the runtime by almost half.
examples.analytical: The narrowing of the historical field leaves the author's claim untested against rival sources.

nuance.analogy: A narrowing is like a funnel: the wide opening at the top gradually becomes a thin stream at the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From narrow, from Old English nearu, plus the suffix -ing, forming a noun of process.
common_mistakes: Confusing narrowing, the process, with narrowness, the state of being narrow.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a separate vowel, 'NAR-oh-ing-uh'.

senses.definition: In a nasty manner.

core.definition: In a mean, cruel or unpleasant way, showing hostility or spite toward someone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short, reduced 'ih', and the final -ly is a quick 'lee'. Pronounce the a as in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes hostile or spiteful behavior, and it can also describe something unpleasantly severe, such as a fall.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nastily mostly to describe how someone speaks, smiles or responds, as in 'she answered nastily'. It is informal and conversational, and it can also describe an injury or accident that was unexpectedly bad, as in 'he fell nastily'. For a polite description you could use rudely or unkindly, which are less emotional.

distinctions.note: Meanly suggests petty, small-minded unkindness, while nastily suggests open hostility or unpleasantness.
Cruelly implies deliberately causing suffering, while nastily can describe a rude or spiteful manner that is less severe.

examples.everyday: He said something nastily about my cooking, and the whole table went quiet.
examples.professional: The vendor responded nastily to our escalation, which made the call much harder.
examples.analytical: The critic writes nastily about the director, although many of his arguments are sound.

nuance.analogy: Like an elbow thrown in a crowded room: it is sharp, and it is aimed at someone.
nuance.etymology: Formed from nasty plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Spelling it nastyly; the y changes to i before -ly, so the spelling is nastily.
Using it for something that is simply disappointing rather than hostile or unpleasant.

senses.definition: To bring a private company, or an industry comprising such companies, under the control of a specific government.
senses.example: The government plans to nationalize the energy industry.

senses.definition: To bring a concept such as a political issue or commercial campaign to the attention of the entire country.
senses.example: The campaign managers hoped to nationalize the slogan so every voter would hear it.

senses.definition: To change from having local and regional variation to being national in character and scope.
senses.example: Over the decades, regional dialects gradually nationalized into one standard American English.

senses.definition: (rare) To make into, or to become, a nation.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To bring a private company or industry under government ownership and control; also, to make a local issue national in scope.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ize is pronounced like the word 'eyes'. The middle syllables are quick, reduced vowels, so say them lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics and politics, but often charged, since it can signal either public benefit or government overreach depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nationalize mostly in economics and politics, for example when the government nationalizes a bank or railroad. In the second sense, a campaign or issue can be nationalized when it spreads from local concern to a national debate. In casual speech people often say the government took over, which is more natural.

distinctions.note: Privatize means the opposite: moving a government-owned business into private hands.
Federalize means placing something under federal or central government control, which is narrower than nationalize, although the two are sometimes used interchangeably.

examples.everyday: Some people wanted the government to nationalize the power company after the outage, but others said it would make things worse.
examples.professional: If the board's plan fails, the government may decide to nationalize the regional airline to keep the routes running.
examples.analytical: A local controversy can be nationalized when activists link it to larger questions about national identity and public responsibility.

nuance.analogy: To nationalize something is like moving a family recipe from one kitchen to the national cookbook: it leaves the local circle and belongs to everyone under one authority.
nuance.etymology: From national, from nation, from Latin natio, plus the suffix -ize, to make or bring into a state.
common_mistakes: Using nationalize to mean simply making something more popular; it usually refers to ownership or to a national scope of concern.
Pronouncing the middle syllables too strongly; the main stress is on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Smart and fashionable.
Natural, as opposed to steroid enhanced.
senses.example: natty gains

senses.definition: National.
Someone whose muscle gains are natural and not aided by the use of steroids.
senses.example: The natty lifter's gains were slow but steady compared with the juiced competitors.

senses.definition: A national championship.
senses.example: I hope my favorite team makes it to the natty this season.

core.definition: Neat, smart and fashionable in dress or appearance; also informally, a drug-free bodybuilder.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle t is a flap that sounds like 'd', so it is close to 'NAD-ee', with a short, light ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful; it praises neat, stylish dress and can sound a little old-fashioned or dapper.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, natty is mostly used in writing or older speech, and it often describes men's suits or dapper details, as in 'a natty little bow tie'. It is not common in everyday conversation, where sharp or stylish sounds more natural. The bodybuilding sense, meaning natural and drug-free, is uncommon and informal.

distinctions.note: Stylish is the common everyday word for fashionable; natty adds a neat, tidy and slightly dapper flavor, often for a man's suit.
Dapper is close in meaning and describes a neat, smartly dressed man, often in a slightly old-fashioned way.

examples.everyday: Your brother looks really natty in that new blazer.
examples.professional: Our new vendor's sales rep arrived in a natty suit, which set a formal tone for the meeting.
examples.analytical: The novel's natty protagonist, always perfectly tailored, becomes a symbol of social performance.

nuance.analogy: Natty is like a well-cut suit with no loose threads: small, neat and deliberately sharp.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to neat.
common_mistakes: Using natty to mean naturally talented; that meaning belongs to a natural.
Pronouncing it NAY-tee with a long a; the vowel is short, as in cat.

senses.definition: A person who navigates, especially an officer with that responsibility on a ship or an aircrew member with that responsibility on an aircraft.
senses.example: The navigator on our flight plotted a course around the storm and told the pilot.

senses.definition: A sea explorer.
senses.example: The medieval navigator charted coastlines no European had recorded before, guided by stars and luck.

senses.definition: A device that navigates an aircraft, automobile or missile.
senses.example: The car's navigator rerouted us onto the highway after the bridge closed.

senses.definition: A user interface that allows navigating through a structure of any kind.
senses.example: Use the navigator on the left side to jump between chapters and sections quickly.

senses.definition: A laborer on an engineering project such as a canal; a navvy.
senses.example: The navigator dug the canal beside the river, working ten hours a day for little pay.

core.definition: A person who plans and directs the route of a ship, aircraft, or vehicle, or a person who reads directions for a driver.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAV, the first syllable, with a weaker stress on GAY. The final syllable is a rhotic r-colored vowel, so say tur, not tor or tor-uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical job or role word with no negative or positive loading.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, the navigator is the passenger who reads the map or directions while the driver focuses on the road. In aviation and the military, navigator is a formal crew role, though modern aircraft often use computers for the job. Civilian drivers may say 'You be the navigator' in a casual way.

distinctions.note: The pilot controls the aircraft, while the navigator plans the route and monitors position, speed, and heading.
The driver operates the vehicle, while the navigator reads directions and tells the driver where to turn.
A guide leads people through a place in person, while a navigator plots a path through space or along a route.

examples.everyday: Can you be the navigator and tell me when to turn? The phone keeps cutting out.
examples.professional: Our navigator module recalculates the route whenever traffic data changes, so drivers get updates in real time.
examples.analytical: Medieval navigators relied on dead reckoning, and their errors in estimating distance shaped the voyages that followed.

nuance.analogy: A navigator is like the map-reader on a hike: the walker keeps moving, while the navigator watches the terrain and calls out the next turn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin navigator, from navigare 'to sail'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, saying NAV-ih-GAY-tor instead of NAV-ih-gay-tur.
Using navigator to mean a driver, when the navigator is the person giving directions.

senses.definition: A newborn infant; recently born baby.
senses.example: The neonate was placed under a warming lamp in the hospital's special care unit.

core.definition: A newborn baby, usually one under four weeks old, used mainly in medical contexts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, NEE. The final syllable rhymes with 'mate' and is not reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. Doctors and nurses use it without emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say neonate mostly in hospitals, medical charts and health news. Friends and family say baby or newborn. Using neonate at a dinner table can sound overly technical, though it is not wrong.

distinctions.note: Infant is a general term for a baby in the first year; neonate is specific to the first weeks after birth.
Newborn is the everyday word; neonate is the clinical term for the same child.

examples.everyday: The nurse said the baby is a healthy neonate, so we can take her home tomorrow.
examples.professional: The team logged every neonate admitted to the unit during the winter surge.
examples.analytical: The clinical definition of a neonate turns on age, not on the child's readiness for life outside the womb.

nuance.analogy: A neonate is like a freshly printed page: it has just come off the press, and everything about it is new.
nuance.etymology: From Latin neonatus, 'newly born,' from neo- 'new' and natus 'born'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'nee-oh-NATE' with stress on the last syllable.
Using neonate for any baby; the word refers only to the first weeks of life.

senses.definition: A very stressed and anxious person.

core.definition: A person who is extremely anxious, stressed, or upset, often from worry or overwork.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on wreck, the second word, while nervous keeps a weaker stress on its first syllable. The w in wreck is silent, so start the word with a clear r sound, not w.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative and often humorous; it is usually said with sympathy about yourself or a friend.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nervous wreck for someone visibly stressed before an exam, interview, or big event, as in 'I was a nervous wreck all morning.' It is casual and often said about yourself with a little self-deprecation. A natural reply is 'Oh, you'll do fine,' or 'Don't worry, it's over now.' For a more formal setting, say 'I was very anxious.'

distinctions.note: Anxious is neutral and describes worry about something, while nervous wreck is an exaggerated, informal image of someone falling apart.

distinctions.vs: wreck (noun, a ruined ship or car)
distinctions.note: Wreck alone can mean a crash or ruin; in this idiom it only describes a frazzled person.

collocations: a nervous wreck before the interview
a nervous wreck over the kids

examples.everyday: I was a nervous wreck waiting for the test results.
examples.professional: Honestly, I was a nervous wreck before our board presentation, but the numbers held up.
examples.analytical: Calling the candidate a nervous wreck describes his manner, but it tells us nothing about the quality of his reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone at one percent battery with every app open, a nervous wreck runs on fumes and jumps at every notification.
nuance.etymology: Nervous comes from Latin nervosus, 'sinewy'; wreck comes from Anglo-Norman wrec, from Old Norse vrak.
common_mistakes: Writing 'nervous wrack', a spelling that is uncommon in modern American writing.
Using nervous wreck for a feeling; for a feeling, say 'I feel nervous' or 'I'm nervous.'

senses.definition: Modeled on the arrangement of neurons in the brain.
Of, or relating to the nerves, neurons or the nervous system.
senses.example: neural connections

core.definition: Relating to nerves, neurons or the nervous system, or to the brain's signaling cells.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The r is clearly pronounced in American speech, and the final syllable is a weak 'ul', not 'ahl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Neural is mainly a technical or medical word, so it appears in science, medicine and computing. Everyday speakers prefer 'nerve' or 'brain' phrases. In AI conversations, neural usually refers to artificial networks.

distinctions.note: Nervous describes feeling anxious; neural describes the physical nerves or neurons themselves.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the numbness was from a neural problem in my hand.
examples.professional: Our team studies neural signals to improve the sensor's accuracy.
examples.analytical: Descriptions of consciousness that ignore neural architecture risk missing the material conditions of thought.

nuance.analogy: Neural is to nerves as 'cardiac' is to the heart: it names the system that carries signals.
nuance.etymology: From Greek neuron, meaning 'sinew' or 'nerve'.
common_mistakes: Confusing neural with nervous, which means anxious or tense.
Pronouncing it with a long a, as in 'NAY-rul'.

senses.definition: An aggregate of neurons.
senses.example: Researchers identified a nidus of neurons in the brainstem that controls breathing.

senses.definition: A nest for insects or small animals.
senses.example: The wasp built a small nidus of mud beneath the porch eave.

senses.definition: A place of infection in an organism.
senses.example: The doctor traced the fever to a nidus of infection in the left lung.

senses.definition: An origin (originating point) for a phenomenon.
senses.example: Historians consider the city's textile mills the nidus of the labor movement.

senses.definition: A home or place to stay.
senses.example: The old boathouse became a nidus for stray cats during the harsh winter.

core.definition: A focal site in the body, such as a patch of tissue or a cluster of cells, where a disease, infection, or abnormal activity begins.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NYE. The final -us is a reduced vowel, so say it like dus, not doos or dus with a long u.

nuance.connotation: Negative in medical contexts, since it describes the place where something harmful begins.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nidus mainly in medical, biological, and scientific writing, where it refers to the origin point of an infection or abnormal activity. In everyday speech, people say source, focus, or site of infection. In biology, nidus can also mean a nest, but that sense is rare outside technical texts.

distinctions.note: Focus is a general word for a central point; nidus is a technical term for the specific biological site where disease or activity starts.
A lesion is any area of damaged tissue; nidus specifically describes where an infection or abnormal process originates.
Nest is the everyday word for a shelter built by birds or animals; nidus can mean that in biology but is usually a medical term.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the infected tooth was the nidus for the whole problem, so she removed it.
examples.professional: The investigation traced the outbreak to a single nidus in the processing plant before it spread to other departments.
examples.analytical: Historians of medicine describe the crowded ward as a nidus where hospital infections took root and spread across the city.

nuance.analogy: Like a patch of weeds that spreads through a garden: the problem starts in one small spot and then takes over the whole area.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nidus, meaning nest.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it NID-us, with a short i, instead of NYE-dus.
Using nidus as a casual word for nest in everyday English, which sounds technical and out of place.

senses.definition: A very unpleasant or frightening dream.
senses.example: I had a nightmare that I tried to run but could neither move nor breathe.

senses.definition: Any bad, miserable, difficult or terrifying situation or experience that arouses anxiety, terror, agony or great displeasure.
senses.example: Cleaning up after identity theft can be a nightmare of phone calls and letters.

senses.definition: (rare) A demon or monster, thought to plague people while they slept and cause a feeling of suffocation and terror during sleep.
senses.example: Medieval villagers feared the nightmare, a demon said to sit on sleepers' chests.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) A feeling of extreme anxiety or suffocation experienced during sleep; sleep paralysis.
senses.example: Grandma swore she had a nightmare every winter, waking unable to move or breathe.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To experience a nightmare.
senses.example: After the horror movie, she nightmared about shadows under her bed.

senses.definition: To imagine (someone or something) as in a nightmare.
senses.example: I try not to nightmare the worst outcomes before the biopsy results come back.

senses.definition: To trouble (someone or something), as by a nightmare.
senses.example: The ghostly stories nightmared the children long after the campfire had burned out.

core.definition: A very frightening or unpleasant dream, or any terrible, stressful or difficult experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NITE strongly. The second syllable is unstressed, so 'mare' reduces to a short 'mer' sound and does not rhyme with 'hair' or 'care.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals fear, distress or extreme annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'It was a nightmare' about anything exhausting or chaotic, such as traffic, a moving day or a broken computer system. The sense of a dream is still the core meaning, and the informal use is very common in conversation. The verb form is rare and mainly literary.

distinctions.note: A nightmare is more intense and frightening, often waking the sleeper, while a bad dream may be merely unpleasant.
A dream can be neutral or pleasant, while nightmare always implies fear or distress.

examples.everyday: Driving downtown on a Friday afternoon was a total nightmare.
examples.professional: Migrating the old database was a nightmare, but the new pipeline is stable now.
examples.analytical: For many Puritan writers, the fear of damnation haunted their lives like a recurring nightmare.

nuance.analogy: A bad dream that refuses to end, even after you wake up.
nuance.etymology: From night and mare, the mare being an Old English word for a goblin or demon that was thought to sit on sleepers.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'mare' like the female horse, with a full 'air' vowel.
Using 'nightmare' for a small annoyance, when it suggests something very bad.

core.definition: A man in the Hebrew Bible, the father of King Jehu of Israel, or sometimes a grandfather of Jehu in the genealogy.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, NIM. The final syllable rhymes with 'my', so the name ends in a long I sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name with no emotional charge in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Nimshi in Bible study or Sunday school, where it appears as a family name in the account of Jehu. Speakers usually say 'Jehu, son of Nimshi' when introducing him.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school we learned that Jehu was called the son of Nimshi, not the son of his own father.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan for the Kings series, Jehu is introduced as the son of Nimshi, which helps students follow the royal genealogy.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'son of Nimshi' in 2 Kings identifies Jehu through a family name, a practice that signals his dynastic and military identity.

nuance.analogy: Nimshi is like a family name on a ballot: it tells you whose son you are speaking about.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (nim-SHY) instead of the first.
Pronouncing the final syllable like 'shee'.
nuance.biblical_note: Nimshi (Hebrew nimshi) is a personal name, and its meaning is uncertain. In 2 Kings 9:2 and 9:14 Jehu is called the son of Nimshi, and in 2 Chronicles 22:7 the same identification appears. The passages show Jehu being anointed by a prophet's servant to overthrow the house of Ahab, so Nimshi is important mainly as Jehu's identifying father or ancestor.

senses.definition: Something easy, not difficult, not posing problems.
senses.example: Finding this house should be no problem if we use a good map.

senses.definition: Certainly, sure (said when granting a request).
senses.example: Porter, can you help me with my bags? — No problem, sir.

senses.definition: No thanks are necessary; you're welcome (said in response to an expression of gratitude).
senses.example: Thank you. — No problem.

senses.definition: No apology is necessary; think nothing of it (said in response to an expression of regret).
senses.example: I'm sorry. — No problem.

core.definition: Something that is easy to do or not difficult, or a phrase meaning you are happy to help.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PRAH in problem, and the middle syllable is often reduced to a weak 'bluh' sound. The r is clear and rhotic in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly; it reassures people that a request or apology is fine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly in shops, restaurants, offices, and phone calls, for example as a reply to 'Thanks' or 'Sorry.' It is very common, so it often sounds natural in both casual and professional talk, though some people find it overused. Alternatives include 'You're welcome' or 'Sure thing.'

distinctions.note: You're welcome is the more traditional reply to thanks; no problem is more casual and relaxed.
No worries is slightly more casual and common in Australia, while no problem is standard in the US.

examples.everyday: Thanks for picking up the milk. No problem, I was already at the store.
examples.professional: Can you move our call to three o'clock? No problem, I'll send an updated invite.
examples.analytical: The phrase no problem treats a favor as trivial, which can reduce the sense of obligation between people.

nuance.analogy: Like an open door that takes almost no effort to walk through.
common_mistakes: Using 'no problem' as a complete answer to a serious question; it can sound dismissive.
Saying 'no problems' in the plural when the meaning is simply that nothing is wrong.

conversation.text: "Thanks for the ride." "No problem. Anytime."
"Can you move your car a little?" "Sure, no problem."
It's no problem at all. I was going that way anyway.

senses.definition: Containing no more than trace amounts of alcohol.
Not involving alcohol as its cause.
senses.example: The nonalcoholic liver damage in his patient surprised the medical team.

senses.definition: One who is not an alcoholic.
senses.example: The support group welcomes nonalcoholics and recovering drinkers alike to its Thursday meetings.

senses.definition: A nonalcoholic beverage.
senses.example: The bartender poured me a nonalcoholic with lime, since I was driving home.

core.definition: Containing little or no alcohol; in the US, a drink with less than 0.5 percent alcohol by volume.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HOL, with secondary stress on non- and al-. Americans use an ah sound here because of the cot-caught merger, so say HAH rather than HAW.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for drinks, suggesting a healthy or responsible choice; the tone depends on context and can sound clinical with beer or wine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it on menus and labels, as in nonalcoholic beer, wine, or cocktail. Many also say alcohol-free or zero-proof, and beer labels often use NA. For a person who does not drink, Americans say he doesn't drink or he's sober, not he's nonalcoholic. At a party, a natural reply to 'Want a drink?' is 'I'll take something nonalcoholic, thanks.'

distinctions.note: Alcohol-free is the more common everyday label on American drinks, and it puts the focus directly on the absence of alcohol.
Sober describes a person who is not drunk or who does not drink in recovery, so it applies to people, not drinks.

examples.everyday: I'll have the nonalcoholic cider, thanks, since I'm driving home tonight.
examples.professional: The company launched a nonalcoholic version of its drink line to meet demand from customers who want low-alcohol options.
examples.analytical: Researchers compared nonalcoholic and alcoholic beverages in social settings to test whether the social effects of drinking come from the alcohol itself or from the ritual of drinking.

nuance.analogy: A nonalcoholic beer is like decaf coffee: it keeps the taste and the ritual, but the active ingredient is almost gone.
nuance.etymology: From non- and alcoholic, from alcohol, which comes through Medieval Latin from Arabic al-kuhl.
common_mistakes: Saying no alcoholic instead of nonalcoholic in ordinary speech.
Using nonalcoholic to describe a person who doesn't drink; Americans usually say he doesn't drink or he's sober.

senses.definition: Not stationary.
A data point whose statistical properties (mean, variance, covariance) are not constant over time.

core.definition: In statistics, describes a process whose mean, variance or covariance changes over time instead of staying constant.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STAY, the second syllable, and the -ary ending is a light, r-colored air-ee. The -tion part is a short shuh, not shun, which is easy to miss.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical property with no positive or negative value.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and econometrics, Americans call a series nonstationary when its statistical behavior drifts, which can break many models unless the data are differenced or detrended. Outside technical work nobody uses it; people say something is changing or not steady. In casual talk it sounds like jargon, so use it only with technical listeners.

distinctions.note: Stationary means not moving or, in statistics, having constant statistical properties; nonstationary is the opposite and refers only to changing statistical behavior.
A trending series moves in a consistent direction; a nonstationary series can change its variance or other properties even without a clear trend.

examples.everyday: My husband jokes that my work schedule is so nonstationary he never knows where I'll be.
examples.professional: The sales series is nonstationary, so we need to difference it before fitting the ARIMA model.
examples.analytical: A nonstationary process can wander without returning to a fixed mean, which invalidates many standard inference results.

nuance.analogy: Like a river whose level keeps rising and falling in new ways; its past average tells you little about where it will be next.
nuance.etymology: From non- plus stationary, from Late Latin stationarius, 'of a station', from statio, 'standing'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the -tion syllable instead of STAY.
Confusing it with stationery, the paper and envelopes; the two words are pronounced the same but spelled differently.

senses.definition: The state of nonexistence; the condition of being nothing.
senses.example: Staring into the empty desert, he felt a terrifying nothingness pressing against his thoughts.

senses.definition: A void; an emptiness.
senses.example: Beyond the last streetlight lay a vast nothingness of fields and dark sky.

senses.definition: The quality of inconsequentiality; the lack of significance.
senses.example: The meeting's agenda was so full of nothingness that everyone left after ten minutes.

core.definition: The state of not existing; complete absence of anything, or a feeling of being empty and insignificant.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the th is voiceless. The ng in 'nothing' is one sound, so do not add a g after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy and theology, but negative or ominous in everyday or literary use, where it suggests emptiness, despair or a loss of meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy classes, theology, literature and serious discussions of death or meaninglessness, rather than in casual talk. In everyday speech they usually say 'nothing' or 'emptiness' instead. A phrase such as 'reduced to nothingness' sounds dramatic and should be used sparingly.

distinctions.note: Emptiness describes a space or container that has nothing inside it, while nothingness is the absence of being itself.
A void is a gap or empty space, often in a literal or figurative sense, whereas nothingness is an absolute absence with no sense of space at all.

examples.everyday: After the power went out, the house sank into a kind of nothingness, with no sound at all.
examples.professional: After the audit, the team's budget had shrunk to nothingness, so the project had to be shelved.
examples.analytical: Sartre argued that human consciousness introduces nothingness into being, since we can always negate what is before us.

nuance.analogy: It is like the blank page before anything is written: not an empty room, but the absence of any writing at all.
nuance.etymology: From 'nothing' (from Old English nan thing, 'not a thing') plus the suffix '-ness', forming an abstract noun.
common_mistakes: Using 'nothingness' in casual conversation, where 'nothing' or 'emptiness' is much more natural.
Confusing it with 'nothingness' meaning simply 'a small amount', as in 'a nothingness of money'; the word refers to absolute absence.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew Genesis 1:2 describes the early earth with the word tohu (formlessness, emptiness), and the RSV renders it as 'without form and void'. Isaiah 40:17 says that the nations are as nothing before God, a passage about the worthlessness of created power compared with God. 2 Maccabees 7:28, in the deuterocanonical books, has a mother tell her son that God made heaven and earth out of what did not exist, the classic biblical basis for creation out of nothing (Latin creatio ex nihilo). Protestants generally treat 2 Maccabees as apocryphal.

senses.definition: The academic discipline around the scientific study of this process.
senses.example: She earned her doctorate in nutrition, studying how diet affects metabolism and long-term health.

senses.definition: That which nourishes; nutriment.
senses.example: I accidentally ate a worm which was in my apple - my uncle said the extra nutrition would do me good.

senses.definition: The organic process by which an organism assimilates food and uses it for growth and maintenance.

core.definition: The process by which the body takes in food and uses its nutrients for growth, energy, and health; also the science that studies this.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'TRISH.' Americans often drop the y sound after 'n,' so say 'noo' rather than 'nyoo,' and the ending '-tion' sounds like 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests health, care, and well-being.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nutrition' in daily life for food choices, such as 'good nutrition' for kids, and in labels like 'Nutrition Facts.' It is also the name of an academic field, so a nutrition major studies food science and health. Be careful: 'nutrition' is an uncountable noun, so do not say 'nutritions.' For a licensed professional, Americans often use 'registered dietitian' rather than 'nutritionist.'

distinctions.note: 'Diet' means the food a person usually eats, while 'nutrition' describes how that food affects the body.
'Nourishment' is more general and can be emotional or spiritual, while 'nutrition' is usually scientific or physical.

examples.everyday: Kids need good nutrition to focus at school, so pack them fruit and whole grains.
examples.professional: Our wellness program offers free nutrition counseling to employees who want to improve their energy at work.
examples.analytical: Nutrition is best understood as a biological process that links food, metabolism, and long-term health.

nuance.analogy: Nutrition is like the fuel for an engine: the quality of the fuel determines how well the machine runs.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nutritio, from nutrire 'to nourish.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'This food is very nutrition'; the correct adjective is 'nutritious.'
Treating 'nutrition' as countable, as in 'the nutritions in food'; say 'the nutrients' instead.

nutrition.etymology: Middle French *nutrition*, from Old French *nutricion*, from Latin *nutritio*.

senses.definition: A fear of the night, nighttime, or darkness.

core.definition: An intense, persistent fear of the night, nighttime, or darkness, often causing anxiety about being alone in the dark.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, on 'FOH'. The first letter 'n' is silent in some spellings, but it is pronounced in this word: 'nik'. The final syllables are reduced to 'bee-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing an anxiety condition
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nyctophobia' mainly in psychology, medicine, or formal discussions of anxiety. In everyday talk, people say 'fear of the dark' or 'afraid of the dark'. The word is clinical, so it may sound too technical in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Fear of the dark' is the everyday phrase, while 'nyctophobia' is the clinical term for a persistent, intense fear.

examples.everyday: My son has a little nyctophobia, so we always leave the hallway light on at night.
examples.professional: The school counselor noted that some students show signs of nyctophobia during evening activities.
examples.analytical: The author treats nyctophobia as a metaphor for the human fear of unknown spiritual darkness.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashlight that seems to go dim when it's most needed: the mind's fear of the unseen grows in darkness.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nyx, nyktos 'night' and phobos 'fear'.
common_mistakes: Using 'nyctophobia' in everyday speech where 'afraid of the dark' is more natural.
Pronouncing the 'ny' as 'ni' with a long 'i' sound instead of 'nik'.

senses.definition: The form of a noun or pronoun used as the object of a verb or a preposition.

core.definition: The grammatical form of a pronoun (such as me, him, her) or noun used as the object of a verb or preposition.

pronunciation.tip: The noun CASE carries the main stress, while the adjective 'objective' has a lighter secondary stress on JEK. The final -tive is a short 'tiv' sound, not 'teev.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: American grammar teachers use 'objective case' alongside 'subjective case' and 'nominative case,' while many modern grammars call it the 'object form' or 'object case.'
