distinctions.note: A guard usually stays at a fixed post, while a patrol moves around an area on a regular route.
Police is the institution or the officers themselves, whereas patrol is the activity of moving around an area to keep watch.

examples.everyday: The neighborhood watch does a night patrol, so the street has been pretty quiet lately.
examples.professional: The security team runs a patrol of the parking lots every two hours and logs anything unusual in the system.
examples.analytical: Debates about the scope of the border patrol's mandate often hinge on how one defines the border zone itself.

nuance.analogy: A patrol is like a night watchman who walks the same route every hour, not to stay in one place but to notice what has changed.
nuance.etymology: From French patrouiller, 'to paddle in mud,' from patte, 'paw.'
common_mistakes: Using a preposition like 'patrol in the street'; say 'patrol the street' or 'on patrol.'
Confusing 'patrol' with 'guard' when the job involves moving around rather than standing at a post.

patrol.etymology: From French *patrouille*, from Old French *patrouille*, *patouille* (“a night-watch”), from *patrouiller*, *patouiller*, *patoiller* (“to paddle or pudder in water, dabble with the feet, begrime, besmear”), from *patte*, *pate* (“paw, foot of an animal”),…

senses.definition: The act or process of reducing to poverty.

core.definition: The process of reducing a person, household or group to poverty, often through economic loss or unfair conditions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the zay syllable, and the first syllable has a lighter secondary stress. Pronounce the -tion ending as shun, and keep the middle syllables short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a harmful process that reduces people to poverty and can imply injustice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pauperization in economics, sociology, political writing and debate about policy. It describes a process rather than a state. In everyday talk they would say getting pushed into poverty or going broke instead.

distinctions.note: Pauperism names the condition of being a pauper, while pauperization names the process by which someone becomes one.
Impoverishment is a broader, more common word for becoming poor, while pauperization is more technical and often implies dependence on relief.
Immiseration is a term from Marxist and economic writing for gradually worsening conditions, whereas pauperization simply means being driven into poverty.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the pauperization of small farmers in our county started when the mill closed.
examples.professional: Our model captures pauperization among households that lose two incomes within a single year.
examples.analytical: Marx's concept of pauperization, debated since the nineteenth century, describes the worsening material conditions of workers under capitalism.

nuance.analogy: Pauperization is like a slow leak in a tire: the loss may seem small each day, but eventually the whole wheel goes flat.
nuance.etymology: From pauperize with the suffix -ation, meaning the act or process of.
common_mistakes: Using pauperization and pauperism interchangeably.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable instead of the zay syllable.

senses.definition: Constantly complaining, especially in a childish way due to insignificant matters; fretful, whiny.
senses.example: Due to the long wait, there were several peevish patients in the doctor’s waiting room.

senses.definition: Quick to become bad-tempered or cross, especially due to insignificant matters; irritable, pettish, petulant.
senses.example: I would rather figure things out on my own than ask that peevish librarian for help.

senses.definition: Coy, modest. Foolish, silly.
senses.example: She gave a peevish smile and looked away when the compliment came.

senses.definition: Coy, modest.
senses.example: The shy bride gave a peevish blush whenever her cousins teased her about the groom.

senses.definition: Foolish, silly.
senses.example: It was a peevish notion to bet the rent money on a single lottery ticket.

senses.definition: Harmful, injurious; also, mischievous; or malicious, spiteful.
senses.example: The peevish gossip spread through the office and ruined two careers in one week.

senses.definition: Impulsive and unpredictable; capricious, fickle.
senses.example: The peevish weather kept switching from bright sunshine to hail every half hour.

senses.definition: Obstinately in the wrong; perverse, stubborn.
senses.example: My peevish brother refused to admit he had been reading the map upside down.

senses.definition: Out of one's mind; mad.
senses.example: After three sleepless nights alone in the cabin, the hermit grew peevish and talked to the walls.

senses.definition: Of a thing: evoking a feeling of distaste, horror, etc.
senses.example: The peevish smell of burnt popcorn hung in the hallway for hours after the fire alarm.

senses.definition: Clever, skillful.
senses.example: She was a peevish hand at chess, outmaneuvering everyone at the club on Thursday nights.

senses.definition: Synonym of peevishly (“in a peevish manner: whiningly; irritably, petulantly; etc.”).

core.definition: Easily irritated, often complaining in a whiny or childish way about small things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEE, and keep the final -ish short, not 'eesh'. The long ee in the first syllable is the key vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes a person's mood or manner as petty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'peevish' mainly in writing and formal description, such as a critic describing a tone or a novelist describing a character. In casual speech they say 'cranky,' 'grumpy,' or 'whiny' instead. Calling someone peevish can sound judgmental, so use it carefully in conversation.

distinctions.note: Petulant describes sulky childish protest; peevish is more about irritable complaining over small things.
Cranky is informal and everyday; peevish is more formal and written.
Grumpy is mild and playful; peevish is more negative and critical.

examples.everyday: Don't be so peevish; we'll get to the park right after lunch.
examples.professional: His peevish reply to the review comments did not help the discussion, so I asked him to focus on the code.
examples.analytical: Critics sometimes describe a moral complaint as peevish when it hides resentment behind the language of principle.

nuance.analogy: A peevish mood is like a stuck zipper: small, repeated annoyances that keep getting in the way.
nuance.etymology: From peeve, a back-formation; the origin of peevish itself is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'peevish' for someone who is simply angry or hostile; it means irritable and whiny.
Stressing the second syllable; say PEE-vish, not pee-VISH.

peevish.etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English *pievish*, *peuysche*, *pevish*, *pevysh* (“capricious, wilful; perverse, wayward”); further etymology, possibly from one of the following:

senses.definition: A thoughtful or reflective state, especially if sad or melancholic.
senses.example: We left quietly so as not to disturb the widow's pensiveness.

core.definition: The quality or state of being quietly thoughtful, often with a touch of sadness or melancholy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEN. The final '-ness' is a light, unstressed schwa-like 'nus', not 'NESS' with stress. Keep the middle syllable short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly melancholy; it suggests quiet reflection, sometimes sad, and is rarely used for cheerful thoughtfulness.
nuance.usage_note: Pensiveness is mostly used in literary writing, reviews, and descriptions of mood or character. Americans in everyday talk would more often say 'she seemed lost in thought' or 'she had a quiet mood'. It is a formal word, so using it in casual conversation can sound overly bookish.

distinctions.note: Melancholy is a deeper and more lasting sadness; pensiveness is a quieter, thoughtful mood that may pass.
Thoughtfulness often means consideration for others; pensiveness is inward reflection that may not involve anyone else.

examples.everyday: There was a quiet pensiveness in her voice when she talked about her mother's garden.
examples.professional: The team's pensiveness after the outage was healthy, because it led them to ask better questions about the logs.
examples.analytical: Ecclesiastes is marked by a pensiveness that does not resolve into easy answers about the meaning of life.

nuance.analogy: Like a lake at dusk: calm, reflective and a little darker than the noon sun.
nuance.etymology: From pensive, from Old French penser 'to think', plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using pensiveness for cheerful thinking; it usually suggests a quiet or sad mood.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'pen-siv-NESS'.
Confusing pensiveness with thoughtfulness, which often refers to kindness toward others.

senses.definition: The shape of a five-pointed star constructed of five intersecting lines meeting at the vertices, such that a central pentagon and five surrounding isosceles triangles are formed; often with magical connotations; a 5/2 (or 5/3) star polygon.
senses.example: She drew a pentagram on the chalkboard to illustrate the golden ratio in the geometry lesson.

core.definition: A five-pointed star drawn with five connected straight lines, often used as a symbol in magic or religion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PEN. The second syllable is a reduced 'tuh', and the final '-gram' rhymes with 'ham', not 'grame'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in geometry; often negative or mysterious in popular culture, since it is linked with witchcraft and occult symbols.
nuance.usage_note: In math and design, Americans use pentagram to mean a neutral five-pointed star. In popular culture it appears in horror films, tattoos and occult settings, so it can cause concern in religious or workplace settings. In Wicca and some other practices it is a symbol of protection, so context matters a great deal.

distinctions.note: A pentagon is a five-sided polygon; a pentagram is a five-pointed star formed by connecting its diagonals.
A pentacle is a pentagram inside a circle, used specifically in magical practice; pentagram can mean the star alone.

examples.everyday: My roommate has a small pentagram tattoo on her wrist, and she says it's just a design she likes.
examples.professional: For the poster, the designer used a pentagram made from five equal straight lines.
examples.analytical: The Pythagoreans saw the pentagram as a symbol of health, linking it to the golden ratio.

nuance.analogy: Like a sheriff's star, but drawn in one continuous motion of five lines without lifting the pen.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pentagrammon, from penta- 'five' and gramma 'line, letter'.
common_mistakes: Using pentagram to mean a pentagon, which is a different shape.
Stressing the second syllable as in 'pen-TAG-ram'.
Assuming pentagram always carries a magical meaning; in math it is neutral.

pentagram.etymology: From Ancient Greek *πεντάγραμμον*, noun form of the adjectives *πεντάγραμμος* and *πεντέγραμμος* (“five-lined, having five lines”).

senses.definition: Of, or pertaining to, the penumbra.
Implied or logically following from something, but not directly stated.
senses.example: Several penumbral duties followed from the contract, even though no clause mentioned them directly.

senses.definition: Connected to a term, but not essential to its meaning.
senses.example: Her definition of friendship included penumbral features like loyalty, though they were not central to the concept.

core.definition: Relating to a penumbra, or to a partly shaded, uncertain zone at the edge of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NUM. The final -al is a reduced syllable like uhl, and the r is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is descriptive and precise, sometimes suggesting vagueness or edge-states.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use penumbral mainly in astronomy, physics and in careful academic or literary writing. Most speakers would say partial or edge instead in conversation. It is rarely used in ordinary talk about feelings or situations.

distinctions.note: Umbral refers to the fully dark part of a shadow; penumbral refers to the partly shaded outer part.
Vague is a general word for unclear; penumbral suggests a border zone that is partly visible but not fully defined.

examples.everyday: The sky got that penumbral gray look before the storm, so we left early.
examples.professional: The model treats the penumbral zone as a range of uncertainty rather than a hard boundary.
examples.analytical: The argument occupies a penumbral space in which the claim is neither plainly true nor plainly false.

nuance.analogy: Like the faint, blurred edge of a shadow where light and dark gradually meet.
nuance.etymology: From penumbra (partial shadow) with the English adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Confusing penumbral with umbral, which means fully dark.
Stressing the second syllable (pen-UM-bruhl) instead of NUM.

senses.definition: In a penurious manner.

core.definition: In a stingy, very frugal or meager way, or while living in severe poverty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NYUR. The 'ious' ending reduces to 'ee-uhs', so avoid saying 'pen-yoo-REE-us-ly' with a strong fourth syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests stinginess, scarcity or harsh poverty, not careful or modest spending.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use penuriously in speech; they would say 'stingily', 'cheaply' or 'on a shoestring'. The word appears in novels, historical writing and formal reviews, often to describe shabby or underfunded conditions. Using it to praise someone's careful spending would sound odd, since the word carries a negative tone.

distinctions.note: Stingily is an everyday word for giving or spending too little; penuriously suggests severe scarcity or poverty.
Frugally is positive and describes careful, sensible spending; penuriously is negative and suggests meanness or deprivation.

examples.professional: The grant was penuriously funded, so the team had to cut two data sources.
examples.analytical: Dickens portrays the workhouse as a place where children are fed penuriously and cared for grudgingly.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet dripping just enough to keep the pipes from freezing, never enough to fill a bucket.
nuance.etymology: From penurious, from Latin penuria 'want, lack, scarcity'.
common_mistakes: Using penuriously to praise careful spending, when it is negative.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'PEN-yoo-ree-us-lee'.
Confusing penurious with penniless; penurious can mean stingy as well as poor.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to, or having the characteristics of, a phantasm (“something seen but having no physical reality”); imaginary, unreal.
senses.example: She insisted that the phantasmal voice of her late brother came to her during the seance.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to, or having the characteristics of, a phantom (“apparition or ghost”); ghostly, spectral.
senses.example: She insisted that the phantasmal voice of her late brother came to her during the seance.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to, or having the characteristics of, a phantasm (“perception or vision of a living or dead person who is not physically present, often through telepathy”).
senses.example: She insisted that the phantasmal voice of her late brother came to her during the seance.

core.definition: Unreal or imaginary; ghostly, spectral, or like a phantasm or apparition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'taz' (TAZ). The last syllable is weak, like 'mul', not 'mal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to eerie; it suggests something unreal or haunting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'phantasmal' in literature, philosophy and formal descriptions of unreal or ghostly things. In everyday conversation, 'ghostly' or 'unreal' are more natural. It is most common in writing about imagination and perception.

distinctions.note: 'Ghostly' is common and everyday, while 'phantasmal' is more literary and abstract.
'Imaginary' means existing only in the mind, while 'phantasmal' adds a sense of eerie, ghostlike appearance.

examples.everyday: In the fog, the trees looked phantasmal, like they might disappear if I got closer.
examples.professional: The sensor readings were phantasmal, showing spikes that no one could reproduce.
examples.analytical: For Berkeley, material objects are phantasmal in the sense that they exist only as ideas perceived by minds.

nuance.analogy: A phantasmal figure is like a reflection on a window at night: you can see it, but it has no body.
nuance.etymology: From 'phantasm' with the adjective suffix '-al'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, like 'FAN-tas-mal'.
Confusing it with 'fantastic', which means wonderful or extremely good.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to philauty.
senses.example: His philautic habits, admiring his own reflection in every shop window, amused his roommates.

core.definition: Relating to self-love, or to an excessive love of oneself.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the AH syllable, the second syllable of the word. The first syllable has a short 'i' and a secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that self-love has become excessive or self-centered.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word found mostly in older or literary writing about moral character. Americans would say 'self-centered,' 'self-absorbed,' or 'vain' in everyday speech. Use it only when you want a precise, somewhat bookish term for self-love.

distinctions.note: Narcissistic is a psychological term for an unhealthy need for admiration, while philautic is a general, older word for excessive self-love.
Egotistical describes someone who talks about themselves too much, while philautic focuses on love of self as an attitude.
Self-love is neutral or even positive, while philautic is clearly critical.

examples.everyday: Honestly, he can be pretty philautic at parties, always talking about himself and his achievements.
examples.professional: The manager's philautic style made it hard for the team to speak up about their own work.
examples.analytical: Some ancient writers saw philautic self-love as a root of vice, while others saw a healthy form of it as necessary for self-respect.

nuance.analogy: A philautic mind is like a mirror that reflects only itself.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philautia 'self-love', from philos 'loving' and autos 'self'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with philanthropic, which means generous toward others.
Using it for ordinary self-confidence; the word implies excess and is negative.

core.definition: A male given name; in the Bible, the name of several men, most notably one of the twelve apostles of Jesus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FIL. The final syllable is short and unstressed, like 'ip' in 'tip,' not 'eep.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is simply a name and carries no inherent positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Philip as a common given name, often shortened to Phil. In the Bible it refers to several men, so context matters. A natural reply to a question about who he is might be 'He's one of the twelve apostles.'

distinctions.note: Phillip with a double l is a common American spelling for the same name, but the Bible and most scholarly texts use Philip.

examples.everyday: My brother Philip just moved to Denver for a new job.
examples.professional: Philip, our lead engineer, will walk us through the data pipeline changes this afternoon.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel of John, Philip brings Nathanael to Jesus, and his question at the feeding of the five thousand shows his reliance on calculation rather than faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a common name that appears in many families, Philip appears in many biblical stories.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Philippos, 'lover of horses,' from philos (loving) and hippos (horse).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'eep,' as in 'fil-EEP.'
Confusing the apostle Philip with Philip the evangelist or Herod Philip without context.
nuance.biblical_note: Philip is the name of several men in the New Testament. The apostle Philip is listed among the twelve (Mark 3:18), and in John 1:43-46 he is from Bethsaida and brings Nathanael to Jesus. Philip the evangelist, one of the seven chosen to serve, preaches in Samaria and baptizes an Ethiopian official (Acts 8:26-40). Luke 3:1 mentions Herod's brother Philip, a tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis.

senses.definition: An academic discipline that seeks truth through reasoning rather than empiricism, often attempting to provide explanations relating to general concepts such as existence and rationality.
senses.example: Philosophy is often divided into five major branches: logic, metaphysics, epistemology, ethics and aesthetics.

senses.definition: A view or outlook regarding fundamental principles underlying some domain.
senses.example: a philosophy of government; a philosophy of education

senses.definition: A general principle (usually moral).
senses.example: Her core philosophy at work is to never promise a deadline she cannot personally meet.

senses.definition: A comprehensive system of belief.
senses.example: Stoic philosophy shaped much of Marcus Aurelius's thinking about duty and suffering.

senses.definition: Synonym of small pica.
senses.example: Our printer recommended setting the appendix in philosophy, which is smaller than pica.

senses.definition: (rare) The love of wisdom.
senses.example: He studied philosophy not for a career but for the sheer love of wisdom.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (dated) A calm and thoughtful demeanor; calmness of temper.
senses.example: Despite the insults, he bore the news with remarkable philosophy and did not raise his voice.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) To philosophize.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The academic study of basic questions about knowledge, existence, reason and value; also a personal set of beliefs about how to live.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LAH, and the middle syllables are weak, with the -suh- sounding like a quick uh. The final -y is a long ee, not ai.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals thoughtfulness and principle. In casual talk it can sound a bit grand when used for simple personal habits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use philosophy in two main ways: for the academic field (someone majored in philosophy) and for a personal outlook (my philosophy is to keep it simple). In the workplace, a team may describe its approach as its philosophy, as in 'our philosophy is to ship early and fix quickly.' You can say 'That's my philosophy' as a friendly way to explain your approach.

distinctions.note: Philosophy relies on reasoning and argument; religion includes revelation, practice and community, though the two often overlap.
Science tests hypotheses through evidence; philosophy examines the concepts and assumptions that science depends on.
A principle is a single rule or guideline; a philosophy is a broader worldview from which many principles follow.

examples.everyday: My philosophy is that you should always get to the airport early, even if it means waiting around.
examples.professional: Our data governance philosophy is to collect only what we need and document every decision we make about it.
examples.analytical: Hume's philosophy of causation challenges the assumption that we directly observe necessity in the relation between events.

nuance.analogy: A philosophy is like a map of the territory of thought: it does not show every road, but it shows how the land is laid out.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philosophia, 'love of wisdom', from philos 'loving' and sophia 'wisdom'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the academic subject with a personal outlook; 'I studied philosophy' and 'I have a philosophy of life' are different senses.
Pronouncing the word as fil-uh-SOF-ee; the stress belongs on the first syllable after the f, as in fih-LAH-suh-fee.

senses.definition: Pertaining to phrenology.

core.definition: Relating to phrenology, the discredited 19th-century practice of reading character and mental traits from the shape of the skull.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LAH, two syllables before the end of the word. The ph is pronounced f, the -ical ending is a weak 'kul', and the stressed vowel is the short ah of 'hot'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when applied to ideas, since it implies something discredited or pseudoscientific.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use phrenological mostly in history of science, philosophy of science or critiques of bad reasoning. It is almost never used to describe modern neuroscience. Calling a claim 'phrenological' is a sharp way to say it rests on no evidence.

distinctions.note: Physiognomic refers to judging character from facial features; phrenological refers specifically to judging it from the skull.
Neurological describes the modern, evidence-based study of the brain and nervous system; phrenological describes a discredited method.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said the old ceramic heads in the museum were used for phrenological readings.
examples.professional: We cut the phrenological examples from the deck because they have no evidence behind them.
examples.analytical: Phrenological explanations of character assumed that mental faculties were localized and could be read from the surface of the skull.

nuance.analogy: Phrenological reading is like reading a fortune from the shape of a teacup: confident, specific, and not based on any reliable method.
nuance.etymology: From Greek phrēn (mind) plus -logy (study of), with the -ical adjective ending.
common_mistakes: Using phrenological to mean modern brain science; the word refers only to the discredited system.
Placing the stress on the first syllable, as in FREN-uh-LAH-jih-kul.

senses.definition: Having toes that point inwards.

core.definition: Having feet that turn inward, so the toes point toward each other when standing or walking.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on PIJ, with a lighter stress on toed. The first syllable has a soft j sound, and the middle syllable is a quick uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it describes a physical trait but can sound unkind if used to tease someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly for children and adults who walk with inward-pointing feet. Doctors may use the term 'in-toeing' in a clinical setting. Calling an adult pigeon-toed in conversation can sound awkward or unkind, so mention it only neutrally or with a caring tone.

distinctions.note: Bow-legged describes legs that curve outward at the knees, a different structure from inward-turning feet.
Knock-kneed describes knees that touch while the ankles stay apart, which is a separate alignment problem.

examples.everyday: My daughter was pigeon-toed when she was little, but she grew out of it by age six.
examples.professional: The clinic's pediatric team reviewed referrals for children who are pigeon-toed and do not need treatment.
examples.analytical: Describing a child's gait as pigeon-toed sounds clinical, but the phrase hides a complex mix of bone, muscle and family history.

nuance.analogy: A pigeon-toed walk is like a pair of doors that swing in toward each other, rather than outward.
nuance.etymology: From pigeon, referring to the bird's inward-turning feet, plus toed.
common_mistakes: Using it for toes that point outward; the word means inward-pointing feet.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'pij-un-TOHD'; the strongest stress falls on PIJ.

senses.definition: To have an erection that shows through the trousers.
senses.example: Sitting through the romantic film, he couldn't hide that he'd pitched a tent.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: to pitch a tent.
senses.example: We pitched a tent beside the lake before the afternoon storm rolled in.

core.definition: To set up a tent on the ground for camping. It is the usual American phrase for putting up a tent outdoors.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TENT, the last word, with a lighter stress on PITCH. The a is a weak schwa, so say it quickly, as in 'pitch-uh-TENT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a plain outdoor activity and is used in camping talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase whenever they set up a tent, at a campground, in the backyard or at a festival. A common reply is 'Let's pitch the tent before it gets dark.' Avoid using it for other meanings, since the crude sense is slang and can sound inappropriate.

distinctions.note: Set up is the more general phrase and is equally natural, while pitch a tent sounds more like camping language.
To camp means to stay outdoors overnight, while pitch a tent names only the act of setting up the shelter.

collocations: pitch a tent in the rain
pitch a tent by the lake
pitch a tent in the campground

examples.everyday: Can you help me pitch a tent before the rain starts?
examples.professional: Our team will pitch a tent at the trade show booth for the outdoor demo.
examples.analytical: To pitch a tent is to make a temporary shelter from a few poles and fabric, a small act of human ingenuity.

nuance.analogy: Like setting up a temporary house in a few minutes, pitching a tent means building a home for one night.
common_mistakes: Using pitch a tent for a different adult meaning, which is a crude slang sense and should be avoided in most settings.
Stressing PITCH instead of TENT in the phrase.

pitch-a-tent.etymology: From the protruding and sometimes tent-like appearance of an erection through one's trousers or bedsheet.

conversation.text: We pitched a tent near the river and fell asleep to the water.
Have you ever pitched a tent in the dark?
You can't pitch a tent on the beach here without a permit.

senses.definition: An angle formed by two intersecting straight lines.
An angle formed by two intersecting planes, measured by the angle between two intersecting straight lines that are in respective planes and perpendicular to the intersection of the planes.

core.definition: An angle formed by two straight lines that lie in the same flat plane, measured in degrees or radians.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ANG in angle, and plane rhymes with 'rain' with a clear long a. The final -gle is one syllable ending in a syllabic l, so don't add an extra 'uh' and say 'ANG-guh-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plane angle mainly in geometry, trigonometry, physics and engineering. In everyday talk people just say angle, and plane angle appears when they need to separate it from a solid angle, which is measured in three dimensions. Students in US schools learn it early, so you will hear it in classrooms and technical drawings.

distinctions.note: A plane angle lies within one flat plane and is measured in degrees or radians, while a solid angle is a three-dimensional opening measured in steradians.
A dihedral angle is formed by two intersecting planes, whereas a plane angle is formed by two lines in a single plane.

examples.everyday: My geometry homework asks me to find the plane angle between these two lines, and I always mix it up with the solid angle.
examples.professional: The CAD model shows a plane angle of 45 degrees between the two faces, so the bracket should fit the mounting plate.
examples.analytical: A plane angle is defined only within a single plane, which is why it cannot be used directly to describe the opening of a three-dimensional corner.

nuance.analogy: Like the opening of a folding fan lying flat on a table, seen from above.
nuance.etymology: Plane comes from Latin planus (flat, level); angle comes from Latin angulus (corner).
common_mistakes: Confusing plane angle with solid angle, which is measured in steradians and describes a three-dimensional opening.
Pronouncing plane with a short a as in 'plan' instead of the long a as in 'rain'.

senses.definition: An often-quoted saying that is supposed to be meaningful but has become unoriginal or hackneyed through overuse.
senses.example: His speech relied on platitudes about hard work that everyone had heard a hundred times.

senses.definition: A claim that is trivially true, to the point of being uninteresting.
senses.example: Saying that people should be honest is a platitude, but it is not really wrong.

senses.definition: Flatness; lack of change, activity, or deviation.
senses.example: The dull desert landscape stretched in an endless platitude of sand and scrub.

senses.definition: Unoriginality; triteness.
senses.example: The novel's plot was so full of platitude that readers quickly lost interest.

core.definition: A dull, overused remark that sounds wise or meaningful but offers no new insight, such as 'everything happens for a reason.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, and the final -tude is pronounced 'tood,' with a long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests empty or shallow talk, and can sound dismissive if used about someone's sincere words.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'platitude' to criticize a speech, a sermon, or advice that sounds nice but says little. Saying 'That's just a platitude' in conversation can sound harsh, so use it carefully. A natural reply to a platitude is to ask for something more concrete, such as 'What would you actually do?'

distinctions.note: A cliche is an overused phrase in general; a platitude is a broader, often moralizing statement that sounds profound but is empty.
A maxim is a short principle offered as truth; a platitude is a maxim that has become trite through repetition.

examples.everyday: When I told my friend I was stressed about the move, she just said everything would be fine, which was a platitude that didn't help.
examples.professional: The leadership update was full of platitudes about teamwork, with no concrete next steps for our project.
examples.analytical: A platitude survives because it is true enough to be unobjectionable, but its very generality conceals the hard questions a specific case would raise.

nuance.analogy: A platitude is like a greeting card: it sounds kind and familiar, but it rarely fits your particular situation.
nuance.etymology: From French platitude, from plat (flat), originally meaning dullness or flatness.
common_mistakes: Using 'platitude' as a synonym for 'compliment' or 'praise'; it is a negative word for empty remarks.
Saying 'PLAT-i-tood' with a long a; the first vowel is short, as in 'plat.'

senses.definition: In plenty; abundant.
senses.example: His farm, though small, nevertheless allowed him a plenteous supply of healthy food.

core.definition: Existing in large amounts; abundant, especially in a poetic or formal style.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle syllable 'tee' clearly separate. The final syllable is a reduced 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests generous, rich, and sometimes almost sacred abundance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'plenteous' in everyday speech; they prefer 'plentiful' or 'abundant'. You will meet it in poetry, the King James Bible, sermons, and old-fashioned writing. Use it in a letter or a toast to add color, but it would sound stilted in a meeting.

distinctions.note: 'Plentiful' is everyday and neutral, while 'plenteous' is literary and more poetic.
'Abundant' is common and formal, while 'plenteous' is archaic and rich in tone.

examples.everyday: Grandma always said the garden was plenteous after a wet spring, and she was right.
examples.professional: The plenteous data from the pilot program let us skip the expensive second survey.
examples.analytical: The psalmist describes the Lord's mercy as plenteous, emphasizing that divine redemption is not scarce but overflowing.

nuance.analogy: A plenteous season is like a table set for a feast, with more food than anyone can eat.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English plenteous, from Old French plentivous, from plenté 'plenty'.
common_mistakes: Using 'plenteous' in casual conversation, where it sounds old-fashioned.
Confusing 'plenteous' with 'plenty', which is a noun, not an adjective.
nuance.biblical_note: In Psalm 130:7 the Hebrew word rabbah, meaning great or abundant, underlies the idea of plenteous redemption. In Matthew 9:37 the Greek word polys, meaning much or many, describes the harvest as plentiful. Psalm 130:7 says with the LORD is plenteous redemption, and Matthew 9:37 speaks of an abundant harvest and few laborers.

plenteous.etymology: From Middle English *plentewos*, *plentevous*, et al. circa 1300, from Old French *plentiveus* (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from *plentif* (“abundant”), from *plenté* (“abundance”) (Modern French *pleinté*, English *plenty*), from Latin…

senses.definition: Excessive, overabundant, rife; loosely, abundant, varied.
senses.example: The startup's plethoric budget let it hire engineers faster than any competitor.

senses.definition: Full or excessively full.
Suffering from plethora; ruddy in complexion, congested or swollen with blood.
senses.example: Doctors noticed his plethoric face and ordered blood pressure tests right away.

core.definition: Extremely abundant or excessive, often more than is needed or wanted.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, THOR. Many speakers with the cot-caught merger make the vowel sound like 'thor' or 'thahr,' but the word is short and clean.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests excess, so it often describes something that is too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use plethoric in writing or formal speech, such as reports, criticism, or essays. In everyday talk, people usually say 'tons of' or 'way too many.' The medical sense about blood is rare, so in ordinary speech the meaning is overabundance.

distinctions.note: Abundant is neutral or positive and common in everyday English. Plethoric is more formal and suggests overabundance or excess.
Copious is formal and describes a large quantity, especially of notes or information. Plethoric adds the idea of too much.

examples.everyday: Our streaming app shows a plethoric list of shows, and I still can't find anything to watch.
examples.professional: The team's plethoric backlog of tickets makes it hard to tell which issues matter most.
examples.analytical: The author's plethoric citations overwhelm the argument rather than strengthen it.

nuance.analogy: A plethoric supply is like a flooded river: there is so much water that it spills over and becomes hard to control.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin plethora, from Greek plēthōrē, 'fullness,' via the adjective plethoric.
common_mistakes: Using plethoric as a noun, instead of the noun plethora.
Confusing it with 'plenty of' in casual speech, where plethoric sounds too formal.

plethoric.etymology: From Late Latin *plethoricus*, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek *πληθωρικός*, from *πληθώρα* (“plethora”).

senses.definition: And; sum of the previous one and the following one.
senses.example: Two plus two equals four.

senses.definition: With; having in addition.
senses.example: I've won a holiday to France plus five hundred euros in spending money!

senses.definition: And also; in addition; besides (which).
senses.example: Let's go home now. It's late, plus I'm not feeling too well.

senses.definition: A positive quantity.
senses.example: The figures show a plus.

senses.definition: An asset or useful addition.
senses.example: He is a real plus to the team.

senses.definition: A plus sign: +.
Abbreviation of LGBT+
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: Being positive rather than negative or zero.
senses.example: −2 * −2 = +4 ("minus 2 times minus 2 equals plus four")

senses.definition: Positive, or involving advantage.
senses.example: He is a plus factor.

senses.definition: (Of a quantity) Equal to or greater than; or more; upwards.
senses.example: The bus can fit 60 plus kids, but we only get 48.

senses.definition: And more.
senses.example: Her starting salary was fifty thousand dollars plus benefits, which seemed generous.

senses.definition: Electrically positive.
senses.example: A battery has both a plus pole and a minus pole.

senses.definition: To add; to subject to addition.
senses.example: Please plus the tax to each item before you total the receipt.

senses.definition: To increase in magnitude.
senses.example: Our team's monthly sales plus whenever the holiday promotions begin.

senses.definition: To improve.
senses.example: Adding a cup of fresh basil really plusses the flavor of this tomato sauce.

senses.definition: To provide critical feedback by giving suggestions for improvement rather than criticisms.
senses.example: Rather than just criticizing, she plussed my drafts with specific suggestions for improvement.

senses.definition: To sell additional related items with an original purchase.
senses.example: The cashier tried to plus my coffee order with a pastry and extra shot.

senses.definition: To frame in a positive light; to provide a sympathetic interpretation.
senses.example: Her manager plussed the layoffs as an opportunity for the team to grow.

senses.definition: To increase the potency of a remedy by diluting it in water and stirring.
senses.example: The homeopath plussed the remedy by diluting it in water and stirring vigorously.

senses.definition: To increase a correction.
senses.example: The engineer plussed the sensor correction by two degrees to account for drift.

senses.definition: (dated) To give a mark of approval on Google+.
senses.example: Did you see my vacation photos? Go ahead and plus them if you like them.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: In addition to; along with something else. Also used to mean 'and' when adding a fact or benefit.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'uh' vowel, as in 'bus' or 'cup', not the long 'oo'. Do not add a second syllable such as 'plu-suh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually presents an extra benefit, but in careful writing it can sound too casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'plus' all the time in speech to add something good, such as 'the food is great, plus the service is fast'. In writing and formal presentations people often prefer 'in addition' or 'also'. In math, 'plus' is also the word for addition.

distinctions.note: 'And' simply joins items, while 'plus' suggests a bonus or extra advantage added to something already good or important.
'Besides' is more neutral and can also mean 'except' or 'other than'; 'plus' stays focused on adding a benefit or cost.

examples.everyday: The hotel was cheap, plus the breakfast was free, so we booked it for the whole week.
examples.professional: The vendor quoted four thousand dollars plus tax, so we should budget about four thousand three hundred.
examples.analytical: Her thesis is coherent, plus it accounts for the anomalies that earlier accounts simply ignored.

nuance.analogy: 'Plus' works like a small bonus added to your paycheck: the base amount stays the same, and the extra makes the total better.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plus, 'more'.
common_mistakes: Using 'plus' to join two full sentences in formal writing, where 'in addition' or 'also' is better.
Making the verb plural after a singular subject with 'plus', as in 'The cost, plus the fees, are high'; it should be 'is high'.

senses.definition: A layer of material.
senses.example: two-ply toilet paper

senses.definition: A strand that, twisted together with other strands, makes up rope or yarn.
senses.example: She untwisted the old rope and examined each ply for fraying before the climb.

senses.definition: Clipping of plywood.
senses.example: The contractor swept up the ply clippings from the floor after cutting the cabinet panels.

senses.definition: In two-player sequential games, a "half-turn" or a move made by one of the players.
senses.example: He proposed to build Deep Purple, a super-computer capable of 24-ply look-ahead for chess.

senses.definition: A bent; a direction.
senses.example: He followed the trail's ply toward the northern ridge.

senses.definition: To bend; to fold; to mold; to adapt, to modify; to change (a person's) mind, to cause (a person) to submit.
senses.example: The negotiators tried everything, but nothing could ply the union's leaders to accept the offer.

senses.definition: To bend, to flex; to be bent by something, to give way or yield (to a force, etc.).
senses.example: The old wooden plank began to ply under the weight of the heavy stones.

senses.definition: To work at (something) diligently.
senses.example: He plied his trade as carpenter for forty-three years.

senses.definition: To wield or use (a tool, a weapon, etc.) steadily or vigorously.
senses.example: He plied his ax with bloody results.

senses.definition: To press upon; to urge persistently.
senses.example: to ply someone with questions or solicitations

senses.definition: To persist in offering something to, especially for the purpose of inducement or persuasion.
senses.example: to ply someone with drink

senses.definition: To travel over (a route) regularly.
senses.example: to ply the seven seas

senses.definition: To maneuver a sailing vessel so that the direction of the wind changes from one side of the vessel to the other; to work to windward, to beat, to tack.
senses.example: The skipper had to ply upwind for hours to reach the harbor entrance.

core.definition: To keep supplying someone with food, drinks or questions, or to work steadily at a trade or occupation.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds like 'pie' and 'sky', with a long 'eye' vowel. Do not say 'plee' or confuse it with 'plow'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the trade sense; mildly negative when someone is pressed with food or drink to get a favor or make them agree.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ply one's trade' for doing a job regularly, often in a formal or slightly old-fashioned way. 'Ply someone with drinks' suggests giving a lot of drinks to make someone talkative or agreeable. In everyday speech, people more often say 'keep someone supplied' or 'keep offering'. A natural reply might be 'Don't let him ply you with pie!'

distinctions.note: 'Supply' means to provide something needed, while 'ply' suggests persistently offering large amounts, often food, drink or questions, to influence someone.
'Practice' is the everyday word for working at a profession, while 'ply one's trade' sounds more formal and suggests steady, skilled work over time.

examples.everyday: Don't let my uncle ply you with pie, or you'll be stuck on the couch all afternoon.
examples.professional: She has plied her trade in data governance for fifteen years, mostly in healthcare.
examples.analytical: The novelist plies the reader with ironic asides that gradually undermine the narrator's authority.

nuance.analogy: To ply is like a river that keeps moving steadily along its course, never stopping, shaping the land as it goes.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English plien, from Old French plier, from Latin plicare, 'to fold'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'ply' with 'supply' or 'apply', which have different meanings.
Pronouncing it 'plee' or 'plow', instead of the diphthong in 'pie'.

ply.etymology: From Middle English *pleit*, *plit*, *plite* (“a fold, pleat, wrinkle; braid, strand in a braided cord, ply”), from Anglo-Norman *pli*, *plei*, *pleit*, and Middle French *pli*, *ploy*, *ply* (“a fold, pleat; joint in armour; situation, state”), from…

senses.definition: Cooked by poaching.
Obtained by poaching.

core.definition: Cooked gently in simmering liquid, usually water, without boiling, as in poached eggs or poached salmon.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long o. The -ed ending becomes a plain t after the ch sound, so it is not pronounced as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive in cooking, where it suggests a gentle, delicate preparation. The sense of illegally taken animals is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans order poached eggs at brunch, often served on toast or as eggs Benedict. The word also describes fruit, such as pears poached in wine. The sense 'obtained illegally', as in poached game or poached fish, appears mainly in news and conservation reports.

distinctions.note: Boiled food cooks in rapidly bubbling water, while poached food cooks in gently simmering liquid, so eggs keep their shape.
Fried eggs cook in fat in a pan, while poached eggs cook in water without fat.

examples.everyday: I'll have two poached eggs on wheat toast, please, with the yolks still runny.
examples.professional: We need to hold the poached salmon at a safe temperature until service, so please check the timer.
examples.analytical: A poached egg depends on gentle heat, so the white sets around the yolk while the yolk stays liquid.

nuance.analogy: Poaching is like a warm bath rather than a boiling pot: the heat is gentle and steady.
nuance.etymology: From French pocher, meaning to cook in a bag or to steal, from poche, meaning pocket or bag.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a short a, as in 'pawcht'. The vowel is long o.
Using poached to mean boiled, which changes the texture of the food.

senses.definition: Containing sufficient poison to be dangerous to touch or ingest.
senses.example: While highly poisonous to dogs, this substance is completely harmless if ingested by humans.

senses.definition: Of an animal such as a snake or spider, or parts of its body: producing a toxin intended for defensive or offensive use which is usually injected into an enemy or prey by biting or stinging; hence, of a bite or sting: injecting poison.
senses.example: Poisonous snakes should only be handled by experienced professionals.

senses.definition: Negative, harmful.
senses.example: Her poisonous comments made the whole team dread every Monday meeting.

core.definition: Containing enough poison to harm or kill if eaten, touched, or breathed in.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POY, and the final -ous is a reduced sound like 'us', not 'ohs'. Learners often say POY-zon-OHS or stress the last syllable, so say POY-zuh-nus.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes danger, and it extends figuratively to harmful people, ideas, or atmospheres.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poisonous for plants, mushrooms, frogs, chemicals, and gas, and they often say toxic for chemicals in safety or technical contexts. Figurative uses such as a poisonous atmosphere are common in news and everyday talk. Warning someone that something is poisonous is direct but never rude.

distinctions.note: Toxic is the usual technical and safety word for harmful chemicals, while poisonous is more everyday and describes things that harm living things when eaten or touched.
Venomous means an animal injects poison by a bite or sting, such as a rattlesnake, while poisonous means harmful to eat or touch, such as poison ivy or a poison dart frog.

examples.everyday: Don't touch that plant, because it's poisonous, so wash your hands if you handle it.
examples.professional: Please label the cleaning solution as poisonous and keep it on the top shelf, away from the food.
examples.analytical: A poisonous idea is not always false; it can be dangerous because it persuades people to harm one another.

nuance.analogy: Like a jar with a skull label: the danger depends on what is inside, not on how the jar looks.
nuance.etymology: From Old French poison, from Latin potio, 'drink', plus the English suffix -ous meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Saying POY-zon-ohs with a stressed final syllable, when the ending is a reduced 'us' sound.
Using poisonous for an animal that injects venom through a bite or sting; American English says venomous for that.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible uses poison for venom and for harmful speech. Deuteronomy 32:33 describes the wine of a wicked people as the poison of serpents, and Psalm 140:3 pictures slander as venom hidden under the lips, an image Paul applies to human speech in Romans 3:13. James 3:8 says the tongue is full of deadly poison. The Hebrew behind the Deuteronomy image is chemah, meaning venom or heat, and the Greek in James is ios, meaning venom or poison.

senses.definition: Pertaining to polymathy; acquainted with many branches of learning.

core.definition: Having wide and deep knowledge across many fields of learning; characteristic of a polymath.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MATH, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The -th is voiceless, as in 'math', and the ending -ic is a short ik sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring. It can sound pretentious if used about oneself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polymathic mostly in academic writing, book reviews, and profiles of thinkers, as in 'a polymathic scientist'. In casual talk people say 'a Renaissance man', 'really well-rounded', or 'knows a lot about everything'. Calling someone polymathic is a real compliment, implying depth in several fields rather than trivia.

distinctions.note: Encyclopedic describes a large store of facts, while polymathic describes a person with real expertise in many separate disciplines.
Versatile means able to handle many different tasks, often practical ones, whereas polymathic focuses on learning across academic fields.

examples.everyday: My uncle is so polymathic that he can talk about jazz, astronomy, and sourdough baking in one conversation.
examples.professional: We need a polymathic team lead who can move between statistics, product design, and stakeholder communication.
examples.analytical: Leibniz's polymathic output, spanning mathematics, philosophy, and law, challenges modern assumptions about specialization.

nuance.analogy: A polymathic mind is like a Swiss Army knife: many tools, each sharp enough to be genuinely useful.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polymathēs 'having learned much', from polys 'many' and manthanein 'to learn'.
common_mistakes: Using polymathic for general trivia knowledge, when it implies serious learning in several fields
Stressing the syllable -ic or the first syllable instead of MATH

senses.definition: The act by which something is posed.
senses.example: different posings of what was essentially the same question

senses.definition: The act of one who poses or postures.
The act of portraying oneself artificially, usually to make oneself appear grander or to fit in with the crowd; pretense.

core.definition: Holding a pose for a photo or painting, or acting in an artificial way to impress others or appear more important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounce the 's' in pose as a voiced 'z', and end with a short 'ing' rather than 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when it refers to photos or art, but negative when it means pretending to be something you are not.
nuance.usage_note: In photo sessions, Americans say 'posing for a picture' in a neutral way. When someone says 'Quit posing,' they usually mean the person is acting fake or trying too hard to look cool. A natural reply to that accusation is 'I'm not posing, I'm just being myself.'

distinctions.note: Posturing suggests pompous, showy behavior, often in politics or argument, while posing is more about presenting a false image.
Modeling is professional work displaying clothes or bodies, while posing is any act of holding a position, including casual or pretended poses.
Pretending is a general word for acting as if something is true, while posing focuses on displaying an image for others to see.

collocations: posing in front of the camera

examples.everyday: Quit posing and just give me a normal smile, okay?
examples.professional: The team lead asked everyone to stop posing as experts and simply share their data.
examples.analytical: Much of online self-presentation amounts to posing, with curated images standing in for an actual self.

nuance.analogy: Like a mannequin in a store window, posing holds a shape that does not move on its own.
nuance.etymology: From pose (verb), from Old French poser 'to place'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'posing to the camera' instead of 'posing for the camera'.
Pronouncing the 's' in pose as an 's' sound instead of a 'z' sound.

senses.definition: Perhaps; indicates that the proposition may be true (is not certainly false) regardless of any facts or circumstances known to, stated by or implied by the speaker.
senses.example: Possibly, they will make gains in the midterm elections.

senses.definition: In the realm of possibility; indicates that the action may successfully be performed (is not impossible) regardless of any facts or circumstances known to, stated by or implied by the speaker that might limit the performance.
senses.example: I'm much stronger than you, so you can't possibly win.

core.definition: Perhaps; used to say something may be true or may happen, though it is not certain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the -ibly ending is a reduced 'ih-blee'. Learners often say 'pos-uh-bly' with a full vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In polite requests such as 'Could you possibly...?' it sounds courteous and humble.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use possibly casually to mean 'maybe' or 'perhaps' in conversation, such as 'Possibly, but I'm not sure.' It is also very common with 'can't' or 'could' to add emphasis or politeness: 'I can't possibly eat another bite.' A natural reply to a polite request is 'Sure, no problem.'

distinctions.note: Perhaps is slightly more formal and common in writing, while possibly is more frequent in speech and often carries a sense of 'it might be'.
Maybe is very casual and usually one word; it rarely appears with 'can't' or 'could' to add politeness or emphasis.

examples.everyday: Could you possibly give me a ride to the airport tomorrow morning?
examples.professional: We may possibly have the numbers ready by Thursday, but I'd confirm with the data team first.
examples.analytical: The argument may possibly be valid, but its key premise remains doubtful.

nuance.analogy: Possibly is like a weather forecast that says 'might rain': it is an open chance, not a promise.
nuance.etymology: From possible, from Latin possibilis, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using possibly to mean 'possible' in the sense of 'able to be done', as in 'I will possibly finish it'; use 'I may be able to finish it' for that.
Putting possibly before a verb in an unnatural place, such as 'I possibly will go'; the natural order is 'I may possibly go' or 'I might go'.

senses.definition: An interpretation of the Book of Revelation where Christ's second coming will be after the "Millennium", a Golden Age or era of prosperity and dominance of Christianity.
senses.example: Her church taught postmillennialism, believing the Golden Age of Christian prosperity would come before Christ returns.

core.definition: The view that Christ will return after a long era of Christian influence and prosperity, often identified with the Millennium.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on LEN, with secondary stress on 'post.' Say 'pohst' with a long o, and don't drop the t before 'm.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is generally optimistic about the progress of the gospel in history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in theology and church history, where it is contrasted with premillennialism. It was influential in the nineteenth century, when many expected steady progress, and later declined after the world wars. Some Reformed Christians still hold it today.

distinctions.note: 'Premillennialism' places Christ's return before the Millennium, while postmillennialism places it after.
'Amillennialism' sees the thousand years as symbolic of the present age, whereas postmillennialism expects a future golden age before Christ returns.
'Dominion theology' is a movement that stresses Christian rule in society, and some forms are postmillennial but the terms are not identical.

examples.everyday: My professor said postmillennialism was popular in the 1800s because people were so hopeful about progress.
examples.professional: The seminar compares postmillennialism and amillennialism and looks at how each shapes views of culture.
examples.analytical: Postmillennialism holds that the gospel will gradually transform the world, so Christ's return crowns rather than interrupts a Christian age.

nuance.analogy: The gospel spreads like leaven through the whole loaf, and then Christ returns.
nuance.etymology: From Latin post-, 'after' + millennium + -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'post' as 'pos' without the long o.
Confusing it with premillennialism.
Thinking it means that Christ's return is not expected.
nuance.biblical_note: Postmillennialists appeal to Revelation 20:1-6 and to passages about the growth of the kingdom, such as the parable of the mustard seed in Matthew 13:31-32 and the leaven in Matthew 13:33. They also cite Matthew 28:18-20, where Jesus sends the disciples to make disciples of all nations.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology does not teach postmillennialism and does not expect a golden age before Christ's return, reading Revelation 20 in a different way.
The Catholic Church does not teach postmillennialism as doctrine, and rejects literal millennial kingdoms, although it affirms that the Gospel is to be spread to all nations.

Postmillennialism arose among Puritans and some Reformed theologians, and was influential in nineteenth-century revivalism. Today it is held by a minority, mostly in Reformed circles, while many evangelicals are premillennial and others amillennial.

senses.definition: A proponent of postmillennialism.
senses.example: My seminary professor was a postmillennialist who believed the gospel would transform the world before Christ returns.

core.definition: A Christian who holds that Christ will return after a long period of gospel-driven progress on earth, which is called the millennium.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEN, the middle-late syllable, not on 'mil' or 'post'. The 'ni' is 'nee' and the final -ist is short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a theological label, and people use it mainly to describe a position in debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in theology, church history, and discussions of end-times views. It is a specialist label, and people often say 'I'm a postmillennialist' to describe their own view. Explain it when talking with people outside theology.

distinctions.note: A premillennialist expects Christ to return before the thousand years, while a postmillennialist expects him to return after them.
An amillennialist does not expect a literal thousand-year earthly reign, and reads the millennium symbolically or as the present church age.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader is a postmillennialist, so he thinks the world gets better before Jesus comes back.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper I compare the postmillennialist and amillennialist readings of the thousand years in Revelation.
examples.analytical: A postmillennialist must argue that the gospel's progress in history is real and not merely hoped for, or the whole position collapses.

nuance.analogy: A postmillennialist sees the gospel like the leaven in Matthew 13:33, working through the whole batch before the bread is baked.
nuance.etymology: From post- ('after') and millennialist, from Latin mille 'thousand' and annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Confusing postmillennialist with premillennialist; the difference is whether Christ returns before or after the thousand years.
Stressing 'MIL' as in 'POST-MIL-en-ist' instead of stressing 'LEN'.
nuance.biblical_note: The term comes from Revelation 20:1-6, which describes a thousand-year reign of Christ with the saints. The Greek phrase behind it is 'chilia etē' (a thousand years). Key passages: Revelation 20:2-3 describes Satan being bound for a thousand years; Revelation 20:4-6 describes the saints reigning with Christ for that period; Matthew 13:31-33 describes the kingdom growing like a mustard seed and leaven, which postmillennialists read as gradual gospel triumph before Christ returns.

traditions.view: Eastern Orthodoxy does not adopt a fixed millennial scheme. It emphasizes the Second Coming and the age to come, and generally avoids detailed timetables for events.
The Catholic Church does not teach a postmillennial scheme. Augustine's reading, that the thousand years describe the present church age, has been widely influential.

Many Puritans and Reformed thinkers, including Jonathan Edwards, held postmillennial views. In the twentieth century premillennialism and amillennialism became more prominent, and some modern Reconstructionists hold postmillennialism.

senses.definition: (obsolete) Sovereignty.
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: Sovereignty or supreme power; this sense is now obsolete.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, POH. The middle syllable reduces to 'tuhn', and the final -cy is pronounced 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in its original sense, but in modern use it can sound pretentious or out of date.
nuance.usage_note: This word is obsolete, so you will find it only in old texts or dictionaries. Modern Americans say sovereignty, power, or potentate. Do not use it in speech or writing, except when quoting an older source.

distinctions.note: Potency is current and means strength or power of effect, as in the potency of a drug; potentacy is obsolete and meant sovereign power.
A potentate is a ruler with great power, a person; potentacy is the state or quality of such power.

examples.professional: The memo avoided the old word potentacy and simply stated who held authority over the budget.
examples.analytical: Early modern treatises sometimes spoke of potentacy to describe the sovereign's supreme and unchecked power.

nuance.analogy: Potentacy is a fossil word: useful for reading old books, but no longer in circulation.
nuance.etymology: From potentate, from Latin potentatus 'power, sovereignty', with the suffix -acy.
common_mistakes: Using potentacy in modern speech; say power or sovereignty instead.
Confusing it with potency, which looks similar but is a current word with a different meaning.

senses.definition: Any of the first propositions of a syllogism, from which the conclusion is deduced.
senses.example: The first premise of the syllogism states that all mammals breathe air.

senses.definition: A proposition antecedently supposed or proved; something previously stated or assumed as the basis of further argument; a condition; a supposition.
senses.example: Our whole budget rests on the premise that customers will pay higher prices.

senses.definition: Matters previously stated or set forth; especially, that part in the beginning of a deed, the office of which is to express the grantor and grantee, and the land or thing granted or conveyed, and all that precedes the habendum; the thing demised or granted.
senses.example: The lawyer read the premises of the deed aloud, describing the land and its boundaries.

senses.definition: A piece of real estate; a building and its adjuncts.
senses.example: trespass on another’s premises

senses.definition: The fundamental concept that drives the plot of a film or other story.
senses.example: The premise of the sitcom is a family running a failing bakery in Ohio.

senses.definition: To state or assume something as a proposition to an argument.
senses.example: The professor premised her lecture on the assumption that markets are not perfectly rational.

senses.definition: To make a premise.
senses.example: We can premise the argument on last year's sales figures.

senses.definition: To set forth beforehand, or as introductory to the main subject; to offer previously, as something to explain or aid in understanding what follows.
senses.example: She premised her remarks with a brief history of the company's founding.

senses.definition: To send before the time, or beforehand; hence, to cause to be before something else; to employ previously.
senses.example: The clerk premised the orders so the stock would arrive before the holiday rush.

core.definition: A statement or assumption that an argument starts from; a basis from which a conclusion is drawn.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PREM-. The final -ise is pronounced like the s in miss, not like the z in wise. Be careful with the verb, which is pronounced prih-MYZE with stress on the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical word for reasoning, but people also use it in everyday talk to describe a basic assumption.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use premise in arguments, debates, business plans and writing about logic. In casual speech, people often say idea, starting point or assumption instead. The word can sound academic if used in ordinary chatter, so use it when you are discussing reasoning.

distinctions.note: An assumption is taken for granted, often without proof. A premise is stated openly as the starting point of an argument.
A conclusion is what follows from premises. The premise is the reason or starting statement.

examples.everyday: The whole plot of the movie is based on a silly premise, but it is fun to watch.
examples.professional: Our forecast model depends on the premise that user behavior will stay stable next quarter.
examples.analytical: The argument fails because its first premise assumes what it is trying to prove.

nuance.analogy: A premise is like the foundation of a house; if it is cracked, the rest of the structure is at risk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praemissa, something sent before, from praemittere, to send in advance.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final s as z, as in premise rhyming with wise; the noun ends in an s sound.
Using premise as a verb with the noun stress, instead of the verb form prih-MYZE.

premise.etymology: From Middle English *premise*, from Old French *premisse*, from Medieval Latin *premissa* (“set before”), feminine past participle of Latin *praemitto* (“to send or put before”), from *prae-* (“before”) + *mitto* (“to send”).

senses.definition: In a series of works, an installment that is set chronologically before its predecessor, especially the original narrative or (perhaps improper usage) any narrative work with at least one sequel.
senses.example: The prequel explains how the villain became a tyrant before the events of the first film.

core.definition: A story, film, or book that is set earlier in time than an existing work and explains events that came before it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PREE. The second syllable is a weak, reduced vowel, so it sounds like kwul, not kwel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, descriptive term used in entertainment talk, often with interest or mild excitement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word freely in conversation about movies, TV shows, video games, and books. You might say The new show is a prequel to the original series. Some purists object to using it for any story with a sequel, but in everyday American speech the meaning is simply an earlier story.

distinctions.note: A sequel follows the original story in time, while a prequel comes before it chronologically, though it may be released later.
A spin-off follows a side character or related story in a new direction, while a prequel is set earlier in the same continuity.

examples.everyday: Have you seen the prequel to that show yet, or should we start with the original season?
examples.professional: The studio is developing a prequel that explains how the main character first joined the company.
examples.analytical: The prequel rewrites the original myth by showing the founder's early failures, which changes how readers interpret his later choices.

nuance.analogy: A prequel is like the first chapter of a family history that was written after the rest of the book was already famous.
nuance.etymology: A blend of pre- before and sequel, following or continuation.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel, like PREE-kwel.
Using prequel to mean any earlier event rather than an earlier story or work.

conversation.text: The prequel tells the story of how the villain got started.
I didn't know it was a prequel until halfway through.
Do I need to watch the prequel first?

senses.definition: Omission; failure to do something.
senses.example: Her pretermission of the safety briefing caused the delay in the lab's experiment.

senses.definition: Preterition; the act of passing over; paralipsis.
senses.example: In the sermon, the pastor's pretermission of the difficult passage surprised many members.

core.definition: The act of leaving something out or failing to do it, often through oversight or by passing it over.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MISH, with a secondary stress on the first syllable. The 'mis' is short, and '-sion' sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and academic use, but it implies a failure of duty when used of a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears mainly in legal writing, such as 'pretermitted heir' in wills and probate, and in older theological or literary prose. In everyday speech say 'omission', 'oversight' or 'something we left out'.

distinctions.note: Omission is the common everyday word for leaving something out, while pretermission is more formal and often legal.
Oversight suggests an accidental mistake, whereas pretermission is a more formal term that can cover deliberate or accidental omission.
Preterition is the theological term for God passing over some people in predestination, and is more common than pretermission in religious writing.

examples.professional: The audit flagged a pretermission of two required approval steps in the release checklist.
examples.analytical: In probate law, pretermission of a child in a will raises the question whether the omission was intentional or accidental.

nuance.analogy: Like a skipped stitch in a quilt: the pattern is still there, but one piece is missing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praetermittere, 'to let pass, to omit', from praeter 'past' and mittere 'to send'.
common_mistakes: Confusing pretermission with 'permission'.
Using pretermission in casual speech, where 'omission' or 'oversight' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A common casual answer: "fine, good".

core.definition: A casual American answer to 'How are you?' or 'How was it?' meaning fine or good, though not outstanding.

pronunciation.tip: The phrase is stressed on 'GOOD', with 'pretty' lighter. Its first syllable is 'PRIT', and the final vowel of 'pretty' is a quick reduced 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive. It sounds friendly and low-key, though a little less enthusiastic than 'great'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pretty good' in everyday small talk as a relaxed reply to 'How's it going?' or 'How was your weekend?'. It signals that things are fine without over-sharing. Its meaning can shift slightly with tone: said flatly it can mean 'okay'. A natural follow-up is 'Yeah? What's new?' or 'Glad to hear it.'

distinctions.note: Great sounds more enthusiastic and positive; pretty good sounds relaxed and modest.
Not bad is a casual understatement that suggests mild approval; pretty good is slightly warmer and more definite.

examples.everyday: Hey, how's your week going? Pretty good, thanks. Just busy with the kids.
examples.professional: How did the client call go? Pretty good, I think. They want a revised proposal by Friday.
examples.analytical: A reply like 'pretty good' signals social politeness rather than a precise report of a person's state.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant meal that fills you up without being memorable: satisfying enough, and nothing to complain about.
nuance.etymology: 'Pretty' as an adverb meaning 'fairly, moderately' has been used in English since the 1500s, and 'good' is Old English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pretty well good' or 'pretty good' with the wrong stress, shifting it to 'PRIT' only.
Using 'pretty good' to mean very good; in American speech it is more modest than 'really good'.

conversation.text: "How are you?" "Pretty good, thanks. How about you?"
The tacos here are pretty good. You should try the fish ones.
I'm pretty good at remembering faces, but terrible with names.

senses.definition: The interest rate that large commercial banks charge on loans to customers with a high credit rating, i.e. those seen as at low risk of default.
senses.example: The bank raised its prime rate, so our variable mortgage payment went up.

core.definition: The benchmark interest rate that large US banks charge their most creditworthy corporate borrowers, and that many consumer loans are based on.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RATE, and prime has a lighter secondary stress. The r in rate is pronounced clearly in American English, and the final t is a flap in phrases like 'the prime rate is'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a financial benchmark term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear prime rate in news about the Federal Reserve and in discussions of credit cards, home equity lines, and variable-rate loans. Most consumers do not pay the prime rate directly; it is the starting point for their rate, often plus a margin. A natural reply when someone mentions a rate increase is 'Oh, so my card's going up too?'

distinctions.note: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other overnight and is set by the Federal Reserve; the prime rate is a bank benchmark that usually sits about three points above it.
A mortgage rate is the interest on a home loan; it may be fixed or variable, while the prime rate is a reference point for many variable-rate loans.

collocations: the Wall Street Journal prime rate

examples.everyday: The bank called to say my credit card rate is going up because the prime rate rose.
examples.professional: The treasury team modeled our variable-rate loans against the prime rate, which moved up half a point after the Fed's announcement.
examples.analytical: Because many variable-rate consumer loans are pegged to the prime rate, changes in the central bank's policy rate pass through to households quickly.

nuance.analogy: Like the benchmark price of a commodity: other prices are quoted as a number above or below it.
nuance.etymology: Prime comes from Latin primus, 'first'; rate comes from Medieval Latin rata, 'fixed amount', from Latin pro rata, 'in proportion'.
common_mistakes: Thinking everyone pays the prime rate; it is a benchmark, and most borrowers pay it plus a margin.
Confusing prime rate with the federal funds rate, which is a different, lower rate set by the Federal Reserve.

senses.definition: The doctrine that, in the absence of certainty, probability is the best criterion.
senses.example: Her seminar on moral theology compared probabilism with stricter approaches to conscience.

senses.definition: The casuistic doctrine that, in difficult matters of conscience, one may safely follow a doctrine that is probable, e.g. approved by a recognized Doctor of the Church, even if the opposite opinion is more probable.

core.definition: Roman Catholic moral doctrine that, in doubtful matters of conscience, one may follow a probable opinion even against a more probable one.
